#2795. Nvidia stock suffers longest weekly losing streak since 2012 as market value sinks by $1.7 trillion

Nvidia investors turned bearish before this week's Jensen Huang saga. But the selling on Wall Street accelerated in the past few days, sending the stock to its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest losing streak since 2012.

The chip giant, which spent most of the year as the world's most valuable company, has lost 30% of its value during the losing streak. That's a drop of roughly $1.7 trillion in market cap and it pushed the company below Apple.

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and led it for 33 years, resigned on Thursday after two separate extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and the other with an employee — were made public. The board named finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a full-time successor.

Nvidia shares fell 13% this week, the most since April 2025. News of the first reported affair hit the front pages over the weekend, when Huang sent a letter to employees apologizing for being "unfaithful to my wife." The board convened late Wednesday after The New York Times reported on the other affair, this one with the company's vice president of health care.

By early Thursday morning, Huang was out, capping a stunning fall for the Nvidia co-founder, who had emerged as one of President Donald Trump's top allies in the corporate world.

"With the unfortunate departure of CEO Jensen Huang we expect a challenging transition for NVIDIA over the next few months," Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, wrote in a report on Thursday. Luria lowered his price target to $200 from $300, but maintained his buy rating. "We believe the market has appropriately adjusted for this transition," he wrote.

Last week, prior to Huang's departure, Nvidia shares dropped about 9%. Much of the decline came after the midterm elections, which resulted in sweeping victories for Democrats and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the artificial intelligence buildout.

In the weeks before the election, Nvidia's stock was sliding alongside the rest of the AI trade on concerns that rising interest rates would punish debt-heavy companies. While Nvidia is wildly profitable, big customers like neoclouds are reliant on the debt markets.

Heading into next week, the pressure is on Kress. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. Analysts are projecting 91% year-over-year revenue growth to $108.9 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era.

Analysts at Oppenheimer wrote in a report on Thursday that, even though they see the company reporting solid earnings, "we expect fundamentals to take a backseat near term."

"The departure of Mr. Huang could, in our view, translate to a lingering share overhang," they wrote.

#2794. Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance—2 habits that take 'a few seconds' can help you avoid similar traps

The biggest heist in cryptocurrency history began with small mistakes many internet users make. A hacking group tied to North Korea recently stole $6.3 billion from the crypto exchange Binance. The operation was sophisticated, involving fake job interviews and malicious code.

But it was also mundane. Although artificial intelligence played a role in the hack, this was not a cyberattack of the future, propelled by swarms of AI agents. Rather, it relied on humans who made some basic errors, like clicking a link because it appeared first on a search results page or trusting strangers at a fake company without taking a few seconds to look them up.

We work at the Digital Inquiry Group, a nonprofit that researches how people evaluate online information and creates free, evidence-based curriculum that helps people decide what to trust.

In over a decade of research, we've found that people frequently engage in online behavior that makes them more likely to get duped. Two simple strategies can help you better navigate today's information landscape, from traditional phishing to misleading social posts to AI fakes. Here's how.

The Binance heist began when one of the company's engineers downloaded compromised software. That engineer, according to the Reuters investigation of the hack, clicked on a sponsored search result that appeared higher on the results page and directed them to the malicious code.

Our research at the Digital Inquiry Group suggests internet users frequently behave as if first is best. They click on the first thing they see. They incorrectly associate a higher placement with vetted content, ceding judgment to tech company algorithms. Students have gone so far as to tell us "Google is almost never wrong" or "AI is always right."

Professional fact-checkers commonly practice click restraint. They understand that whether you're searching on the internet or querying a chatbot, first isn't always best. If you're researching an organization, the first link will often be to its own site, which is hardly likely to disclose anything that's wrong with it.

So the next time you search for something online, be wary of links to sponsored content, the organization you're investigating, or to open platforms where anyone can post and information isn't verified, such as Quora or Reddit. Read the brief snippets beneath each link, and make a more informed choice about what to open.

Always ask yourself: Who is behind this information? What makes them credible? Look for people and organizations that have direct expertise on the topic at hand, or have processes to ensure the accuracy of information, such as news outlets that employ editors and fact-checkers.

Binance says it caught that first malicious download, replaced the device and changed passwords. But later, another engineer downloaded compromised code as part of what they thought was a job interview, which included a virtual meeting with the supposed CEO of a fake company.

It's tempting to think that the engineer should have seen something was off. But the internet is a precarious place because bad actors know how to make content feel legitimate. Binance says its employee was snared by a hacker posing as an HR rep who "shared a social media account with him, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in order to build trust."

When they encounter a piece of unfamiliar content, professional fact-checkers don't just read it closely — they read laterally. They open new browser tabs to see what other, credible sources have to say. Fact-checkers know that bad actors make themselves look good on their home turf, but that it's a lot harder to fake a good reputation across the internet.

The next time you encounter something unfamiliar online, look for authoritative sources that can shed light on the person or organization. You might find a news article that confirms the claim you're looking into, or a report that identifies a supposedly neutral source as biased.

In some cases, you may find nothing at all, which is a signal in itself: if you look up a company that reached out to you and find no external confirmation of its existence, that should be an immediate red flag.

Had that first Binance engineer engaged in click restraint and verified the source of the software, they might have avoided the malicious download. Had that second employee taken time to seek external verification about the supposed HR rep, rather than trusting a polished social media profile, they might have realized that something didn't add up.

The internet and AI have made it harder to know whether what we see is authentic. They've also made it easier than ever before to investigate who or what we encounter online. It's always worth pausing to check. A few seconds up front can save us all a lot of time, grief and money later on.

Nadav Ziv is a researcher at the Digital Inquiry Group. Joel Breakstone is co-founder and executive director of the Digital Inquiry Group.

#2793. Rapid Recap: Magic 107, Bucks 99

The Milwaukee Bucks fall to 0/2 in the NBA Cup and 1-12 overall, losing to the Orlando Magic 107-99 in a game that was at least competitive. Jaime Jaquez Jr. led the Bucks yet again with 22 points off the bench on 8/15 shooting and 5/7 from three. Franz Wagner starred for the Magic, dropping a near triple-double of 35 points, 12 assists, and nine rebounds (at one point it was a triple-double, but they apparently retracted a rebound).

With Ousmane Dieng getting the surprise start, the Bucks began slowly, with Myles Turner turning the ball over twice in the first two possessions and the team going 1/5 from the field and 1/4 from the charity stripe as the Magic led 12-4 at the seven-minute mark. Milwaukee responded, however, with a 10-3 run, thanks in large part to Kel'el Ware, who impacted early with a put-back slam and a corner triple. We even got treated to first-quarter Gary Trent Jr. minutes, but his elite defence couldn't stop Franz Wagner, who carved up the visitors in the pick-and-roll as the Magic took a 23-15 lead into the first major break.

Wagner continued to kill the Bucks early in the second, nailing two threes to extend Orlando's lead to 13 just over two minutes in as Milwaukee's shooting woes continued. Thankfully, a select few Bucks were shooting well, including Myles Turner, who nailed his third three of the night to cut the deficit to 10 with seven minutes to play. After starting 0/5, Tyler Herro began to cook as the second wore on, hitting a three, a floater, and a few free throws as the Bucks inched closer, down 34-28 halfway through the period. Unfortunately, the Magic closed on an 18-8 run as their balanced attack dominated the Bucks on both ends, leading 52-36 at the half.

Coach Jenkins started Nate Ament in Dieng's place to start the third, and the rookie paid that faith off, opening the quarter with a corner three after going 1/6 in the first half. In general, the Bucks looked much more fluid on offence, but they couldn't get stops as Desmond Bane punished them twice from deep to give his side a 65-45 edge four minutes in. The visitors wouldn't give in, though; they knuckled down on defence, which allowed them to play more in transition and go on a 10-0 run. That said, the Bucks had major free throw issues, making just 7/15 (!) midway through the third. That's when Bane really started to cook, knocking in a three plus the foul, then another three on the next possession as the margin blew back out to 16. Jaime Jaquez Jr. was huge to close the quarter, though, nailing multiple bombs and a mid-range shot to keep the Bucks within shouting distance, down 84-72 after three.

It was a frantic start to the fourth, with Milwaukee giving up plenty of open looks but the Magic failing to hit any; as a result, the visitors kept their deficit around 10 as they lived at the line. The Magic's lead stayed around that margin for the next four minutes as the Bucks' parade to the charity stripe continued (though they kept missing when they got there). In fact, Milwaukee didn't hit a field goal for over six minutes, but remarkably, they remained (somewhat) in the game. In the end, though, Wagner was too much, leading his side to their first home victory of the season.

The Bucks were atrocious from the free throw line, making just 18 of 31 attempts in a game they lost by eight. Kyle Kuzma shot a staggering 7/15 on his own!

I physically cannot watch Kuzma-ball anymore, man. It's buyout time (even though I get that he has no incentive to want that).

#2791. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

#2789. Miles Russell got within 1 shot of Austin Championship lead, ends 3 back

With a deft stroke and another birdie buried in the bottom of the cup at the sixth hole of the Omni Barton Creek Resort Canyons course, Miles Russell found himself as close to the lead in a PGA Tour event as any time in his life in the third round of the Austin Championship on Nov. 14.

Russell, an 18-year-old Jacksonville Beach native who began the third round in a tie for ninth, four shots behind Trace Crowe, had already made his fourth cut in five starts this season. A 9-under 135 beat his previous best 36-hole PGA Tour score by two shots as he posted opening rounds of 67-68.

Three birdies in his first six holes put him in a tie for third, one shot behind Crowe. Russell's bid to climb higher faltered with a double bogey at the par-4 ninth hole but the weekend's not over yet and he finished with a 71 for a 54-hole total of 10-under 206, in a tie for 14th at the time he signed his card, three shots behind co-leaders Crowe, Erik Van Rooyen and Chad Ramey.

Russell made only one more birdie after the sixth hole, a two-putt from 36 feet at the par-5 14th hole, and bogeyed the par-5 18th after a visit to native grasses on the left of the fairway.

That's where Russell got into trouble at the ninth hole, with his second shot finding a penalty area. But he's executed many more good shots than not in his ninth PGA Tour start and his fifth of the season.

Russell has made 16 birdies, the product of hitting 43 of 54 greens (79.6 percent). He's also hit 73.8 percent of his fairways (31 of 42).

It's already been a big week for Russell. On Nov. 9 he was named the American Junior Golf Association boys Player of the Year for the third time, a feat equaled in the past only by Phil Mickelson, and on Nov. 11 he signed a letter of intent to play golf at Florida State, the key piece of the puzzle to give the Seminoles the top recruiting class in the nation.

Russell is well on his way to topping his best PGA Tour performance, a tie for 39th in the U.S. Open. His best showing in a Korn Ferry Tour event was last March with a tie for 15th in the Club Car Championship in Savannah.

#2788. Knicks’ valiant comeback against Pacers falls short with NBA Cup reign likely kaput

INDIANAPOLIS — About a year prior, Jalen Brunson nailed a stepback, game-winning 3-pointer in the final seconds against the Pacers.

On Friday night inside the same Gainbridge Fieldhouse, a nearly identical situation presented itself, but coach Mike Brown instead called on Karl-Anthony Towns. Captain Clutch was a decoy on the other side of the court. The result was a fadeaway miss off the rim from KAT, a 106-104 Knicks defeat and probable end to New York's NBA Cup defense.

"I thought it was a great shot. I was excited for the opportunity," Towns told The Post. "I got to make a quick decision. It's either OG is open on the rip screen and he has an open layup or I get to take the shot. I just was ready for the opportunity. … I'm happy with the follow through. I was happy with the technique. It just wasn't my day."

Karl-Anthony Towns (32) of the New York Knicks handles the ball against the Indiana Pacers in Indianapolis on Nov. 13, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

The Knicks launched an improbable comeback to reach that dramatic conclusion, recovering from an eight-point deficit in the final 90 seconds because Indiana kept coughing up possessions.

With 2.8 seconds remaining, the Pacers threw away an inbounds pass — largely because of Mikal Bridges' hounding defense — which set up KAT's opportunity.

Jalen Brunson of the New York Knicks plays defense during a game against the Indiana Pacers in Indianapolis on Nov. 13, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

"We needed a 2-pointer. We had executed something like that in practice," Brown said. "We thought we would gain an advantage with a little rip screen. KAT got a great look. Probably a shot that he makes nine out of 10 times. So I'm okay with it.

"Karl-Anthony Towns' big chance bounced off the rim."

Technically, the Knicks aren't eliminated from the NBA Cup with an 0-2 record. It's still theoretically possible to win the group or a wild-card spot with a 2-2 record. But in the NBA Cup's three-year history, no team has advanced with anything less than a 3-1 mark in the group phase.

The Knicks are the lone squad in their five-team group without a win.

New York Knicks center Karl-Anthony Towns (32) reacts to a call against the Indiana Pacers in Indianapolis on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

There's still much more time to defend their bigger championship, but the Knicks (6-6) hardly have looked like the juggernaut of their magical run of May and June.

They missed 30 3-pointers and gave up 17 offensive rebounds in Indiana, the place of several Knicks heartbreaks over the past few years.

Brunson dropped 33 points with 11 assists — including a powerful third-quarter burst after being motivated by taunts from Pacers defender Quenton Jackson — but Captain Clutch went cold in the fourth quarter and wasn't involved in the final play.

New York Knicks guard Jalen Brunson (11) shoots as Indiana Pacers guard Andrew Nembhard defends in Indianapolis on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Towns finished with 23 points and 15 rebounds, breaking a 56-year franchise record with his 12th double-double to start a season. He eclipsed Willis Reed's mark from 1970 and then came up just a little short with an opportunity to extend New York's NBA Cup hopes.

"That play was something we liked, and we went to it. But I'll say this: That play did not cost us the game," Brown said. "We were lucky a little bit, and our guys did fight to give us a chance down the stretch. But I don't care who you play, it's going to be hard to win a game on the road when you lose the possession game like we did, if we get blown by on defense as bad as we did, if you let your opponent win the physicality battle like we did. It's all a recipe for a loss. And that's where I'm disappointed."

#2785. Ecuador wants to monetize its biodiversity — while still drilling for oil

Ecuador, known for its "megadiverse" Galapagos Islands, Amazon rainforest, Andes and Pacific coast, wants to protect its natural landscapes for years to come — but it faces a tricky balancing act.

As well as preserving its nature, the South American country also plans to capitalize on its critical minerals and continue to extract oil from parts of the Amazon — both of which have led to protests from Indigenous and environmental groups.

One way Ecuador is planning to channel funds into its nature is via new financial tools, such as "debt-for-nature" swaps and its first sovereign green bond. It is also aiming to raise its environmental profile on the global stage by hosting the U.N.'s biodiversity summit, known as COP18, in 2028.

Ecuador, which uses the U.S. dollar, is no stranger to green finance. In March, IDB Invest, the private-sector arm of the Inter-American Development Bank, and Ecuadorian lender Banco Bolivariano issued a $120 million biodiversity bond to back conservation projects. The government also completed two swaps in 2023 and 2024 — deals in which a country's debt is refinanced on better terms in exchange for commitments to spend the savings on conservation. Together, they freed up about $1.1 billion for conservation in the Amazon and Galapagos Islands.

Juan Carlos Blum, Ecuador's minister of environment and energy, said the country hopes to issue sovereign green bonds for the first time in 2027, to raise finance to protect its coastal and mountainous regions and the people whose livelihoods depend on them. The government is looking to the European Union for advice on such instruments, he said. The bloc set green bond standards in 2024.

For Blum, one of the challenges is public awareness. "A lot of us are not aware of how we depend on nature, how we depend on the biodiversity, how vulnerable we all are towards climate," he told CNBC by video call.

Another challenge for Ecuador, as it looks to protect its biodiversity, is its reliance on oil.

The country is a significant oil producer in Central and South America and in October, the government announced plans to open up new tenders for oil exploration in parts of the Amazon, according to local media reports. The news was reportedly met with criticism from Indigenous leaders, who strongly oppose the plans.

"We are being careful on that balance between biodiversity and natural resources use, renewables or not renewables, and it's a delicate matter," Blum said. "That's my day-to-day reality, dealing with balancing this."

About 80% of Ecuador's energy was generated from oil and oil products in 2024, according to the International Energy Agency, while about two-thirds of its electricity was produced using hydroelectric power.

Cracking down on illegal mining is a focus for Blum, who told CNBC he was aware of the environmental impact of legal mining, but that illegal mining was a far bigger problem.

At Ecuador's first Bio Summit held Nov. 4 to Nov. 6 in Quito — an event aimed at helping the country's natural assets "enter the global financial system" — a new way of monetizing nature was introduced.

Marcelo Salame, the event's president, told CNBC he is working on a project to bring so-called biodiversity credits to the country for the first time, to "preserve and monetize" a 260-hectare, or 640-acre, area of the Prosperina forest owned by ESPOL University in the port city of Guayaquil.

Salame said biodiversity is "multidimensional," with credits reflecting a whole ecosystem rather than carbon emissions alone.

Biodiversity credits work in a similar way to the carbon credits that large companies buy to meet sustainability goals, but track a range of measures such as the number of species in a given area or tree canopy cover, with the money raised funneled back into nature protection.

But whereas carbon credits can be used to offset emissions, biodiversity credits cannot. "It's all about funding verified nature outcomes and not, to date at least, compensating for damage," Martin Vaquié, co-founder of Berlin-based Bloomlabs, a company that tracks the biodiversity market, told CNBC.

Jerry Toth, a conservationist and co-founder of Ecuador-based Third Millennium Alliance, a nonprofit that aims to protect the "last remnants" of Ecuador's Pacific Forest, told CNBC that carbon markets can reduce the ecological value of a forest to a single metric: how many tons of carbon it stores.

"That can be potentially dangerous because then you have people that are optimizing for this one metric at the expense of all the other things," he said. Toth hopes biodiversity credits can capture the nuances of an ecosystem.

Toth also runs chocolate maker To'ak — which made headlines for producing the "world's most expensive chocolate bar" — using ancient Nacional cacao grown in Ecuador's Manabí province and processed in Quito.

Third Millennium Alliance works with farmers to restore degraded land by planting cacao in the shade of taller trees, and To'ak pays them around $1.20 per pound of cacao, about double the current market price, Toth said.

Ensuring that chocolate production does not deplete nature is "the key question," Toth said. "Our goal at the outset was, how do we use chocolate to reverse deforestation?"

Ecuador recognizes its "immense" ecological and biological resources, Toth said. "It's still trying to figure out how to … capture that value in a way that makes sense both for people in Ecuador and for the ecosystem."

#2783. Miami Dolphins offensive line review: Tracking the guards in Week 9

When you lose 19-9 in a game where your offense only crosses midfield a handful of times, it's usually best to burn the tape and move on.

That may be especially true for the offensive line, where rookie left guard Kadyn Proctor and second-year right guard Jonah Savaiinaea remain key pieces of the Dolphins' future. While the offense struggled as a whole, player development doesn't stop because of one ugly afternoon, and that's especially true for two young guards expected to be part of the foundation moving forward. Each week, we take a closer look at Proctor and Savaiinaea and examine what analysts are saying about their most recent performances.

Listen, it was not a good week for the offensive line – if you were hoping for a bounce-back effort after a rough outing against the Patriots, the tape from the Detroit Lions game offered very little comfort. While much of the post-game attention has been directed toward Aaron Brewer and Austin Jackson, the entire unit struggled against a physical Detroit front. Alain Poupart over at Sports Illustrated called the offensive line the team's most disappointing position group based on PFF rankings (I know, I know):

Brewer is ranked 17th out of 36 qualifying centers.

Jackson is ranked 71st out of 71 tackles. That's not great, Bob.

Jonah Savaiinaea is 69th among 75 guards.

For Kadyn Proctor, while it was undeniably a rough afternoon against the Lions, there is still plenty of reason for long-term optimism. His individual tape showed some correctable rookie mistakes, such as getting too flat on a second-quarter power play and completely missing his linebacker assignment. However, he also flashed his high-end potential later in the game by quickly recognizing a slanting defensive tackle on a trap concept and stopping on a dime to seal the block. While there were instances of missing second-level blocks, Proctor still played with physicality and had some highlight blocks. He continues to flash the talent that made him a first-round pick, and his mistakes largely look like growing pains.

The conversation around Jonah Savaiinaea, however, is becoming a bit more concerning. The Lions frequently isolated him in space by putting five men on the line of scrimmage, and Jonah struggled mightily, particularly when giving up inside moves. On one notable power play, indecision caused Jonah to completely pass up his assigned defender, blowing up the timing of the run. After a solid first three weeks of the season, his recent tape has looked a lot like his 2025 rookie struggles, when he ranked last among all guards. While it is still too early to make a definitive call on his career trajectory, it's fair to ask if he may settle in as a below-average starter rather than the long-term answer we hoped for. Maybe we'll see more of that early-season tape against the Colts.

The tracker will be updated each week throughout the season. For a more in-depth breakdown of Proctor's and Savaiinaea's performance, check out offensive line Coach Eric Smith's film analysis of the game, which you can find on his YouTube channel, Focused on Fins.

#2782. Division II team loses conference title game after time management meltdown forces OT

The Kentucky State Thorobreds and Benedict Tigers met on Saturday for the Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Conference (SIAC) championship game.

The game went to overtime, but not before the Thorobreds had an all-time meltdown with the clock.

Kentucky State had first-and-goal from the 4-yard line in a 45-45 game with 56 seconds left. When the final whistle sounded, though, Kentucky State hadn't even fully lined up to attempt a game-winning field goal.

The Thorobreds ran the ball on first down for a 2-yard loss. It looked like they were just lining up for the expected field goal attempt, but that is not what happened.

The players walked around, showing little urgency. The broadcast then cut to Thorobreds head coach Felton Huggins Jr., who realized with 12 seconds left on the play clock that he needed to get his kick team on the field because his team had no timeouts left.

At that point, 20 seconds remained on the game clock. Kentucky State ran out its kicking team, but because the offense hadn't gotten the message and had already lined up to run another play, they didn't leave the field until about six seconds remained on the play clock.

Kentucky State ran out of time and was whistled for a delay of game with nine seconds left on the game clock. The penalty brings with it a 10-second runoff. So, despite having nearly a minute to work with, the Thorobreds ran just one play and didn't even attempt a game-winning field goal.

Benedict led 14-7 in the first quarter, but Kentucky State then scored 31 consecutive points to build a 24-point lead. Benedict battled back, tying the game at 45 with 3:15 to go.

After Kentucky State failed to move the ball in what looked like its final possession in regulation, the Thorobreds punted. The Tigers muffed the punt, and Kentucky State took over at the 17-yard line. After getting down to the 4-yard line, it looked like the game was over, with the Thorobreds just needing a field goal to win.

After the clock mismanagement, Benedict scored a TD in overtime, and Kentucky State couldn't match it. The Tigers won the SIAC championship, their third in program history.

#2779. Nvidia is done with Jensen Huang. The fallout in Washington is just beginning

Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia. Washington is just getting started with him and the company he co-founded.

Huang, the leather-jacket-clad CEO of the world's most important chipmaker, resigned from Nvidia on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. But the spy saga is gripping Washington, and lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged U.S. artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet.

Republicans will have their chance first during their last six weeks controlling both chambers of Congress. GOP leaders immediately summoned Huang to Capitol Hill and said they would subpoena him if he doesn't agree to show up. In January, Democrats, who are already eager to make their mark with oversight when they take over the U.S. House and Senate, will be in the driver's seat.

"In this environment where there's some really high stakes when it comes to our national security, I would expect there would be some follow-up, yeah," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday.

Huang and the woman with whom he reportedly had a relationship, Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean technology company Megaspeed and an alleged Chinese spy have drawn congressional attention. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn fire after reports this week that he stalled President Donald Trump's crackdowns on firms routing Nvidia chips to China.

Some Congress members have also called for an investigation into the role of the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of the Commerce Department that manages and enforces export controls, in the Huang scandal.

The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, claimed in emails to Commerce investigators probing Alice Huang's company that he'd been in touch with Jeffrey Kessler, who leads BIS. The Commerce investigation into Megaspeed, which allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China, was then transferred to the Justice Department.

By Thursday night, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick to testify before his committee in December. Later that same night, Lutnick had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement.

Scott threatened to subpoena Huang if he does not appear. A banking panel spokesperson did not immediately respond Friday morning when asked if they'd heard from Huang.

"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology," Scott wrote to Huang. "The American people deserve answers."

And with Democrats poised to take control of both chambers come January, the tech mogul's close ties to the White House will add fuel to an already burning fire as the new majority spools up myriad investigations into the Trump administration.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., in a post to X on Thursday, said "Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk." Schumer is in a contested race to become Senate majority leader in the next Congress.

The senators who will lead those investigations, and hold subpoena power in the new Congress, are gearing up for Nvidia to take center stage.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., the likely incoming chair of the Senate banking panel, said in a statement Thursday that "Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls

Warren and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter Wednesday to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."

Even before Democrats take control in January, Huang is expected to appear before Congress.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., is actively negotiating for Huang to testify before House committees and told reporters Thursday the Nvidia CEO has agreed to appear in the coming weeks.

Details of that testimony are still being worked out, Mast said. It would likely include his committee, as well as the House intelligence panel and the House Permanent Select Committee on China, and it would be under oath and transcribed. It's not clear at this point whether it would be public.

"We want to see him basically in a week … Sooner rather than later," Mast told reporters Thursday, adding that he believed it would happen before Thanksgiving.

If Huang doesn't willingly appear, Mast said he will subpoena him.

Mast, along with House Select China Committee Chair Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., sent a second request Thursday to Huang and Teter requesting they appear and giving them an 8 p.m. ET Friday deadline to respond. Mast also sent a second request to Kessler.

Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., a member of the House Intelligence Committee, said Friday during an appearance on CNBC's "The Exchange" that he wants answers from Huang on the national security and export implications of the affair.

"From an intelligence committee perspective, you can imagine from an AI perspective, how important this is for our national security, for our critical infrastructure and understand when it comes to chip policy, what exactly got to China and ... did Megaspeed divert chips?" Gottheimer said.

The calls for immediate investigation into Huang and Nvidia on the day of his resignation represent a stunning fall from grace in the halls of power for the former CEO. Huang was one of the most effective voices for the AI industry in Washington — able to toggle between leveraging his relationship with Trump and defending his industry from fears about AI's risks to lawmakers.

"He is always the TED Talk guy," one senior Democratic staff member who was granted anonymity to describe private meetings they had attended with Huang, told CNBC. "He's really good and articulate, and really good at explaining why AI is important and why it's so important for the United States to be leading here."

The staffer said Huang was a "happy warrior" for AI, and stayed longer than scheduled or anticipated for questions from lawmakers. But in the meetings with lawmakers the aide attended, they said Huang did not aggressively push against export controls or get too "deep in the weeds" to really "lobby one way or the other" with the lawmakers.

Huang has repeatedly resisted export controls publicly, a move that has rubbed some lawmakers the wrong way.

Some lawmakers even lamented the loss of Huang, despite the inevitable buzzsaw he now faces on Capitol Hill.

"It's just sad all around," Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., said of Huang's resignation.

#2777. High School Football: Cretin-Derham Hall has prayers answered, twice, in stunning win over Northfield

Cretin-Derham Hall looked destined for a third state quarterfinal loss in as many seasons.

Cretin-Derham Hall faced a 4th and 20 from its own 28 yard line, trailing Northfield 27-21 in the final minute. Gavin Russell chucked up a prayer into coverage that somehow found the arms of Owen Welk, who hauled in a 44-yard catch to extend the drive.

Three plays later, Cretin-Derham Hall was again in deep trouble, this time facing a 4th and 9 from the Northfield 27 yard line. Russell took the snap, climbed the pocket to evade pressure and found a wide open Shaheed Suggs by the front left pylon for the tying score with just nine ticks to play.

Jack Cool knocked in the ensuing extra point and Cretin-Derham Hall escaped with a 28-27 victory in the Class 5A state quarterfinals after winning a wild affair.

Fewer than two minutes earlier, Northfield had its own heroics. Northfield faced a 3rd and 9 from the Cretin-Derham Hall 29 yard line with fewer than 90 seconds to play when quarterback Davis Ness rolled out of the collapsing pocket, strolled toward the right boundary and faired a laser to the end zone to Lincoln Wilson for the go-ahead score.

But Northfield missed the ensuing extra point.

Cretin-Derham Hall will face Brainerd in the state semifinals at 7 p.m. next Saturday at U.S. Bank Stadium.

Ness tallied four touchdowns for Northfield — three passing and one rushing. Cretin-Derham Hall's Isaac Feller made two of the key plays for the St. Paul school — tallying an 88-yard kickoff return for a score at the end of the first half, then hauling in an 80-yard scoring strike from Russell to tie the game at 21-21 in the fourth quarter.

Brainerd 14, Spring Lake Park 13: Spring Lake Park trailed Brainerd 14-0 in the final frame Saturday in the Class 5A quarterfinals, and nearly pulled off an improbable comeback.

Nolan Roach hit Jake Wagner for an 8-yard scoring strike to pull the Panthers within seven. The defending state champs then got the ball back, and, on 4th and 11 from the Brainerd 14 yard line, Roach rolled right and hit Kaden Konkler for a touchdown in the front corner of the end zone.

Spring Lake Park went for the go-ahead 2-point conversion, but Roach's was helicoptered near the goal line on his rushing attempt and was marked just short.

The Panthers' managed to recover the ensuing onside kick, but couldn't threaten for the winning score, ending their state title defense.

Mankato West 38, Hastings 21: Gophers commit Zack Shatek scored thrice, including rushing scores of 65 and 48 yards in the second half, but the Raiders couldn't stop the rushing of Mankato West quarterback Osborne Lorenz, who ran in four scores to end Hastings' first state tournament appearance since 2003.

Mankato West will face Monticello in next week's state semifinals.

#2776. Analysis: Companies love a ‘rockstar’ CEO. Until they depend on one

When Jensen Huang quit, it struck me how quickly the conversation shifted from his departure to whether Nvidia could manage without him.

It wasn't about whether the company had the technology, customers or talent to keep growing, but whether anyone else could do what Huang had been doing for the business. That made me wonder: did investors believe in Nvidia, or just Huang?

The company is hardly short of capable people. Interim CEO and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been with Nvidia since 2013. Nvidia has experienced engineers, established customer relationships and a leading position in the artificial intelligence chip market.

But, listening to guests on CNBC this week, I noticed how much of their concern was about the influence Huang had built outside Nvidia.

On Friday, just a day after Huang quit, Dylan Patel of SemiAnalysis told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" how Huang would persuade executives at smaller companies that make critical components to commit capacity to Nvidia. This helped it secure "the majority of supply chain capacity," he said.

Without Huang, competitors could try to persuade those suppliers to allocate more capacity to them, Patel argued. And so the big question is, how much of Nvidia's advantage comes from its technology and how much comes from the relationships Huang built?

There are obvious benefits to elevating CEOs to be rockstars. They can attract investors, open doors and give a company a new identity. A charismatic leader attracts attention, reassures investors and makes a company's strategy easier to sell.

Huang was particularly good at this. He helped shape the conversation about where AI was heading and made Nvidia central to it. Donning his trademark leather jacket, Huang took to stages around the world, courting world leaders to lay out his vision and explain why Nvidia would be at its center.

Before Huang resigned, Eric Ross told "Squawk Box Asia" that Huang "is the company."

That may sound like an endorsement, but it also helps explain why his departure has raised so many questions.

Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon made an interesting distinction on the same program, also before Huang's departure. Nvidia had capable executives who could keep the business running, he said. What was harder to replace was Huang's vision.

"They need a visionary like that," he said.

But for a company whose valuation reflects not just what it sells but expectations of what AI could become, replacing that vision may prove harder than replacing the CEO.

Duncan Clark pointed to another part of Huang's job. He had become a bridge between Silicon Valley, Asia and Washington, and one of the most prominent voices for the wider AI industry.

"I don't think you can replace him with one individual," Clark said on "Access Middle East" on Friday. Replacing him with multiple people is "going to take time, and it won't be the same," he added.

That distinction may be important. Nvidia's board has begun a search for a permanent CEO and said it will consider both internal and external candidates. But whoever takes the job may not personally assume every role Huang had come to play around the company. Some of his responsibilities and relationships could end up being spread across Nvidia's broader leadership team.

For now, the board is emphasizing continuity. New chair Harvey Jones said Kress is backed by an experienced leadership team and that Nvidia expected its operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption. Kress, meanwhile, pointed to Nvidia's people and leadership team as strengths as the company moves forward.

Other boards will be watching, particularly those that have allowed their CEOs to become the face of everything their companies do.

When a charismatic leader is the only person outsiders hear from, it becomes harder to convince them that anyone else can take over. There is also the question of accountability.

Clark described Nvidia's situation as a governance failure. And my colleague, "Squawk Box Europe" anchor Steve Sedgwick, raised a similar point on Friday about how corporate America has approached ESG.

Much of the political debate has focused on its environmental component, Steve said. President Donald Trump has repeatedly attacked environmental and climate policies using phrases such as "green scam." But Steve questioned whether the governance element has been overlooked, particularly at some of America's biggest technology companies.

"When you have a 'Rockstar' CEO you need way more governance, NOT less," he said, citing his recent conversations with CEOs and senior executives.

His point was that powerful leaders can come to believe the normal rules don't apply to them. Without strong governance to challenge them and prepare for their departure, the consequences for a company can be far greater.

Linda Ford, chief executive of The Chartered Governance Institute in the U.K., said Nvidia showed what could happen "when a company's leadership is built around one person." She noted that Nvidia had never previously had a board chair, adding: "A high-profile leader can be an asset, but the board needs to work hard to protect its independence and provide the scrutiny shareholders are entitled to expect."

And that gets to the bigger issue. How easily can a board challenge a CEO who has delivered extraordinary success, particularly when investors have come to see that person as indispensable?

Companies spend years putting leaders in front of investors and customers and making them central to the business. But how much effort goes into making sure the company can function without them?

Nvidia now has to show that the business Huang built can stand on its own. Other boards might want to ask themselves whether they could say the same.

#2775. Pacers 106, Knicks 104: “I’m sure Indiana will look like an all star team tonight.”

Daltong called it. "I'm sure Indiana will look like an all star team tonight." The Hoosiers may have entered the game 4–8 overall and 1–4 at home, but even while weathering the absence of Tyrese Haliburton, they have another gear available to them. For instance, on Veterans Day, when they ripped open the fourth quarter with 14 unanswered points. Or tonight, when they outscored the Knicks (6–6) by 13 early in the final frame and held on for a 106–104 win.

Tonight's tilt at Gainbridge Fieldhouse was another Group B game in the NBA Cup tourney. The Knicks were favored because they're the more talented team on paper, but their effort showed up too late to steal the win. They were simply out-hustled for most of the game. In the positive column, Karl-Anthony Towns registered his twelfth straight double-double (23 PTS, 15 RBS), breaking Willis Reed's franchise record for consecutive double-doubles to start a season. And Mikal Bridges took 12 shots! For 18 points! On the less positive side, Josh Hart went scoreless on four shots, the Knicks lost the paint by 20 and second-chance points by nine, and yet again they attempted double-digit fewer free throws than their opponent (IND 18-of-25, NYK 10-of-13).

Shield your eyes from all this yellow . . . looks a little like a filthy urinal.

The game started inelegantly, with Andrew Nembhard (12 PTS, 4-14 FG, 6 AST, 6 TO) taking the opening tip in for an easy layup. At the other end, Hart thought KAT was going to cut. Instead, KAT crowded Jalen Brunson (33 PTS, 11-22 FG, 11 AST, +8) along the arc, and Nembhard deflected Hart's pass out of bounds. That kind of confusion is predictable this early in the season, especially with Hart having missed a few games already. So is KAT's ability to steamroll Ivica Zubac (12 PTS, 13 RBS) for snacks at the cup.

OG Anunoby (11 PTS, 4-13 FG, +8) laced an early triple when Hart noticed that Pascal Siakam (19 PTS, 5-13 FG) was napping in transition. OG and Pascal have a history, and they made each other's jobs difficult for most of the night. (After that three, OG would make one of his next seven attempts.)

The Knicks took control with a 9–0 run that turned a 9–9 tie into an 18–9 lead. Towns scored seven of those nine and finished the quarter with 12 points and three rebounds. The oft-maligned Bridges chipped in six points and a steal (welcome back!), and Hart had four boards and three dimes. Brunson scored just two points but set up three baskets before picking up his second foul, an offensive foul, and heading to the bench.

Jay Huff brought Indiana back with eight quick points off the bench, including two threes and an alley-oop from that pest T.J. McConnell. Miles McBride answered with a longball, but the Knicks went more than three minutes without scoring after that. Deuce missed his next three attempts, Shamet bricked a couple, and Huff blocked Andre Drummond at the rim. Indiana went on a 15–5 run, taking a 24–23 lead on an OAKAAKUYOAK Obi Toppin bank shot. Towns returned and restored the lead with a driving and-one. The good guys were up 27–26 at the horn.

If you enjoyed the stanky shooting and one-and-dones of the first quarter, the Knicks cordially invited you to more of the same in the second. OG tied it at 31 on another Towns-as-hub laser, then Indy rattled off a 13–4 run. Toppin laced a three and finished a fast break, while Zubac elbowed his way to three O-boards on one possession before putting it in. No Diawara tonight, but Pacôme Dadiet made a brief (as in one minute) appearance in the second.

Yet again, free throws were the biggest bugaboo. In their last game, the Knicks shot 14 fewer free throws than Cleveland. In tonight's second quarter, Indiana went 13-of-17 while New York shot . . . 1-of-2. Call the vet! These zebras have rabies!

Brunson scored half of the team's 22 second-quarter points. Towns grabbed six rebounds but scored just two points, and Josh Hart, Landry Shamet, and Miles McBride all fired blanks. Aaron Nesmith scored six straight, the last on a technical free throw after Mike Brown drew a tech, to stretch Indiana's lead to 14. Brunson hit a turnaround and fed Tyler Kolek for a late three to regain some ground. Indy led 58–49 at the break.

Through the first half, our heroes were dishing the ball fine, with seven more assists than the Hoosiers. Rebounds and points in the paint were basically a dead heat. The voodoo was in the fouls. The Knicks had committed twice as many as the Pacers (14–7). And somehow Rick Carlisle found it necessary to complain about the calls.

On to the third. Cap was cooking, with 16 points and four dimes. The Knicks needed it all and then some. Brunson led an 8–0 run that brought New York within five, but the comeback stalled before they could get back to black. Kelly Oubre Jr. and Nesmith each scored seven in the period, Zubac added six points and five boards, and the hosts were up by 14 again.

From there, the Knicks closed on a 15–2 run to get within a point. McBride hit two bombs, Shamet added one, and Drummond grabbed three defensive boards and a steal. Deuce and Anunoby both missed chances to take the lead in the final eight seconds, so the Knicks went into the fourth trailing 85–84.

From there, two scenarios were possible. Either the Champs would maintain their momentum and turn back those pesky Pacers, or Indy would do what they did against the Wiz on Wednesday and go on some crazy run. 'Twas the latter, fans. After Anunoby tied it at 87, the hosts answered with a 15–2 run. Nembhard scored six points in the quarter, Oubre added five points and two steals, and Zubac finished with nine offensive boards. The Knicks kept fumbling and bumbling the ball away. This time Captain Clutch couldn't save them either, managing only four points in the fourth after scoring 16 in the third.

Behold the bumbling and fumbling of which I wrote:

New York still had a shot to tie it in the final minute. Brunson's layup with 26 seconds left cut the deficit to four, and after Siakam missed both free throws, Bridges (!) hit a pull-up to make it 106–104. Anunoby picked off Siakam's pass with three seconds left, but Towns missed a 15-foot turnaround and the Pacers held on. Ballgame.

If you're feeling testy after another loss, so is Jose Alvarado. Evidently, he and Quenton Jackson have prior history of physical scrapes (including an altercation when Alvarado was still with the Pelicans). Jackson not only taunted Jalen Brunson tonight, but in the third quarter he jawed at Rick Brunson, too. Jose might be out of the rotation, but the big dawg is always ready to defend his captain!

Up to Toronto our heroes go to play the Raps on Sunday. This is your recap, chaps. Safe travels, Knickerbockers.

#2774. Microsoft apologizes for massive outage that took down Outlook and other 365 services

Microsoft issued an apology Friday for a wide-ranging outage that shut down Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products, as the company worked to restore service nearly 24 hours after connectivity problems began.

"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously," a Microsoft spokesperson said Friday.

On Saturday, Microsoft said it had addressed the underlying issue and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions.

The connectivity disruption stemmed from "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade," Microsoft said in a Friday statement. The software giant added that the underlying cause of the outage had been addressed and that they were still working to restore services to some customers.

Engineers scrambled to solve connectivity problems that began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday.

Email and calendar service Outlook, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, were largely down during the morning hours in the U.S. on Friday and throughout the Asian and European business days. Numerous external services that connect with Microsoft products were also hit. Users began to regain access to email and other services Friday morning.

In an update around 10:30 a.m. ET on Friday, Microsoft noted "encouraging recovery progress" and said that "service availability and email delivery performance [was] improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure" as Outlook and other Microsoft 365 tools began to come back online.

In an earlier update Friday morning, Microsoft said that email queues were "approaching normal levels," but that intermittent issues were expected as recovery efforts continue. It had previously given updates by region, with Asia Pacific services among the first to start normalizing.

Engineering teams have been taking affected systems offline for fixes and bringing them back online gradually stages. They are prioritizing efforts to preserve emails delayed during the recovery process and reduce email queues and backlogs, extending the timeout window, whereby delayed emails continue to attempt delivery, to 48 hours to help protect messages.

Microsoft says it has not detected any malicious activity causing the outage, which it initially blamed on a traffic surge in part of its infrastructure and issues with a component responsible for processing server health. The company said it would issue a full report once its assessment of the outage was complete.

The company said in its initial updates on Thursday that the connectivity problems related to infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions," caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure." Some servers were failing automated health checks, it said.

Microsoft shares traded largely flat Friday.

Governments and businesses across the U.S., Asia-Pacific and Europe said they were monitoring the situation, which was causing widespread disruption.

The U.K.'s National Health Service said the outage was affecting some of its services but that patients should attend appointments as normal. Calls "may be subject to long waits" as a result of disruption to the organization, a hospital group serving South West London and the English county of Surrey said on X.

Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov. 12, rescheduled the release to Nov. 16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage.

U.S. Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., told CNBC's "The Exchange" that he asked for a briefing on the outage. Gottheimer worked at Microsoft prior to serving in Congress.

"Is there something that went on that's nefarious here, or is this just something else? These outages occur in a lot of the companies, but the size of it and the length of it and the timing of it," Gottheimer said.

Air India said it had "temporarily rerouted" emails so it could continue to receive customer messages, adding that its flight operations were not affected.

Australian Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said in a press conference that Microsoft "believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Reuters reported.

A fault with an update issued by cybersecurity company CrowdStrike caused one of the world's biggest IT system outages in 2024, hitting airlines, banks and more.

Microsoft reported in 2025 that Copilot, its collection of AI assistants and tools, had more than 100 million monthly active users.

The incident highlights a business "resilience and dependency issue that has been decades in the making," James Owen, managing partner of Digital Risks at consultancy Control Risks, said by phone.

"We have become, organizationally in the private sector and more broadly, increasingly dependent on a smaller segment of technology and infrastructure as critical to daily life and business activities."

"Organizations are becoming more aware through a geopolitical lens about what technologies they adopt, whether their services are provided by firms in the U.S., or China, or elsewhere, but this shows the importance of proper recovery planning in the case of an IT outage. That could be manual backups, protocols that do not require internet connection, investing in diverse suppliers and crisis management planning rehearsals," he said.

Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site on Thursday.

Amazon wrote on X that services were "operating normally" and an "unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports." The company referred users to its health dashboard for "accurate data."

At 4 p.m. ET Thursday, Microsoft said it had "validated an alternative service health check method" that brought some affected servers back online.

"We're now applying this change more broadly," Microsoft wrote. "We're also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses."

#2773. Ohio State WR Jeremiah Smith tops Heisman odds, see stats vs Northwestern

Jeremiah Smith continued his Heisman Trophy push with a strong performance during Ohio State's 28-19 win over Northwestern on Nov. 14.

Smith was key to the Ohio State win. More than half of freshman quarterback Luke Fahey's completions went to Smith, including a 10-yard touchdown pass in the fourth quarter.

Smith helped Ohio State get back in the win column after losing back-to-back games to USC and Oregon.

See Smith's stats and Heisman odds below.

Smith has -145 odds to win the Heisman Trophy, according to BetMGM on Nov. 14 at 4 p.m.

After his odds dipped below those of Notre Dame quarterback CJ Carr last week, Smith's latest performance made him the favorite again.

Smith caught 11 passes for 117 receiving yards and a touchdown against Northwestern.

Smith has 80 receptions for 1,317 yards and 15 touchdowns in the 2026 season.

Smith has 243 receptions, 3,875 yards and 42 touchdowns in his career. Smith also set the Big Ten record for career receiving yards, passing Purdue receiver John Standeford's total of 3,788.

Smith acknowledged before the season began that the 2026 college football season will likely be his last. College football players must be three years removed from high school before declaring for the NFL draft.

An Oct. 7 mock draft from The Athletic's Nick Baumgardner has the Miami Dolphins selecting Smith with the No. 1 pick despite their need for a quarterback.

"Quarterback obviously would be an option for the Dolphins in Round 1, as would a trade. But this idea shouldn't be ruled out. Smith is truly one of the best wide receiver prospects of the past 25 years – possibly beyond," Baumgardner wrote.

A mock draft from CBS Sports' Ryan Wilson also put Smith at the top spot.

Wrote Wilson: "Smith is the best player in college football, and it may not be particularly close. And if the Dolphins feel like Malik Willis is a better option than any of the QBs in this class, Smith is an easy choice here."

The Dolphins are a top candidate to land the No. 1 pick. They released veteran quarterback Tua Tagovailoa and wide receiver Tyreek Hill, and traded wide receiver Jaylen Waddle to the Denver Broncos for multiple draft picks. They are winless this season.

The Dolphins also signed Willis to a three-year, $67.5 million contract with $45 million guaranteed. Willis, a former third-round draft pick, played well as the Green Bay Packers' backup to Jordan Love. In two games as the starter last season, he threw for 409 yards and three touchdowns without an interception while rushing for 104 yards and two touchdowns.

MORE BUCKEYE, LESS AI: Prefer The Dispatch on Google

Despite giving Willis a lucrative deal, there's a chance the Dolphins could still go with a quarterback in the top spot. A mock draft from Sports Illustrated's Justin Melo has Texas quarterback Arch Manning landing with the Dolphins, with Smith landing with the Titans at the No. 2 pick.

If Smith were drafted by the Titans, he would reunite with fellow Buckeyes receiver Carnell Tate, who was selected fourth in this year's draft. A year before that, the Titans selected Miami quarterback Cam Ward with the No. 1 pick.

"Yes, the Titans drafted Carnell Tate last year, but Smith is a near-perfect prospect who would give Ward an even better chance to reach his ceiling," Melo wrote.

Smith and Tate were a dynamic duo during the Buckeyes 2025 season. Smith finished with 1,243 receiving yards and 12 touchdowns last season, while Tate had 875 yards and nine touchdowns.

Johnson crashed the board hard in the first half as well, which led to him getting this and-one opportunity.

Nickeil Alexander-Walker found some life on both sides of the ball to start the quarter, turning defense into offense.

Later on, Dort extended his range beyond the 3-point line to get the Hawks within one point.

The Hawks weren't able to take the lead in the quarter, but they did trail 84-83 going into the fourth.

As much as it felt like the Hawks had life to start the fourth, the Bulls went on an 11-2 run to bring their lead back to double digits. That forced the Hawks to have to fight back again. Johnson took over for the Hawks, willing his way to the paint for easy looks.

McCollum got it going for the Hawks as well, and he was able to tie the game.

It felt like every time the Hawks were in striking distance, the Bulls would hit a big shot, and that's what they did, going on a 7-0 run. That didn't bother the Hawks, more specifically Johnson, who once again put his imprint on the game. He found Okongwu for this 3-pointer, the got some points of his own in transition to tie the game.

With less than a minute remaining, the Hawks got a good shot from Alexander-Walker in transition, but he missed. That gave the Bulls an opportunity to take the lead, but they also missed on their chance.

With 4.0 seconds, the Hawks got another good look, but Wiggins fumbled the ball, and it went out of bounds. That gave the Bulls another chance, but they didn't capitalize, and the game went to overtime.

The Hawks were able to attack first, but that was all they had as Powell took over for the Bulls. Unfortunately, the Hawks couldn't match their energy, and they walked out with a loss.

Johnson finished the game with 27 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists, McCollum finished with 20 points, an Alexander-Walker finished with 16 points.

#2769. After Jensen Huang’s exit, what top financial advisors are doing with Nvidia: Exclusive CNBC poll

Shares of Nvidia continued to slide after the market open on Friday after declining 4% on Thursday following news of co-founder Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive, amid reports about his personal relationships and national security concerns. The news has raised questions for investors about what comes next for a company at the center of the artificial intelligence boom.

To gauge how wealth managers are responding, CNBC polled members of its Financial Advisor 100 and Financial Advisor Council. Thirty of the 122 firms and professionals contacted responded to the online, multiple-choice flash poll, conducted between 11 a.m. and 5 p.m. EST on Nov. 12. The poll is a snapshot of respondents' views, not a measure of all financial advisors.

Most respondents, 19, said they are holding their Nvidia positions steady. Another four said they are increasing their stake, while seven said they do not own the stock. None said they were selling at the time of the poll.

"Most of our clients are in a position to hold; the reason is because it makes up a smaller percentage of an overall diversified portfolio," Winnie Sun, managing director and founding partner of Irvine, California-based Sun Group Wealth Partners, said in an interview. Sun is a member of the CNBC Financial Advisor Council.

Read coverage of CNBC's 2026 Financial Advisor 100 list, including stories featuring ranked firms and their advisors:

In open responses, several advisors wrote that they are taking a "wait-and-see" approach before changing their investment strategy with Nvidia and are telling their clients to do the same.

"Don't react to short-term headlines," wrote certified financial planner Peyton Jamison, president of Jamison Private Wealth Management in Alpharetta, Georgia. "The company's valuation is extremely attractive, and the focus should remain on its underlying fundamentals and long-term investment potential." His firm is ranked No. 78 on the 2026 CNBC Financial Advisor 100 list.

Asked what factors could change their approach to Nvidia, 13 respondents cited the outlook for AI demand, 11 pointed to valuation, and 10 mentioned company leadership or governance. Some said the decision depends on the client, with eight citing risk tolerance and seven mentioning portfolio concentration. Seven said they do not expect to change their approach.

Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results Tuesday, after the market close. In poll remarks, advisors said the company's fiscal third-quarter earnings will help determine their course of action.

Advisors said that for investors, what to do may depend on how much Nvidia stock they already own, when they expect to need the money and how comfortable they are with volatility.

"If this is a company that's going to keep you up at night and you just feel really uncomfortable with these unknown risks, then there was always the option to sell and move that capital to another stock or another portfolio," Sun said.

Nvidia exposure can also come through mutual funds and ETFs. Nvidia's large market value makes it a significant holding in many broad-market funds, including funds that track the S&P 500, as well as target-date funds in retirement-plan options.

Investors can check their Nvidia exposure by reviewing the fact sheets for the funds in their 401(k) or brokerage accounts, which typically list a fund's largest holdings. A stock's decline does not translate one-for-one into a fund's decline.

However, investors with dedicated technology, semiconductor or growth funds may have more Nvidia exposure than they realize, advisors say.

"Nvidia is a big part of virtually everyone's portfolio whether they take an active or passive index approach," wrote Andy Pratt, a partner and director of investment strategy at Burney Wealth Management in Reston, Virginia, which is ranked No. 34 on the 2026 CNBC Financial Advisor 100 list.

He said he advises clients not to overreact to short-term news and to let the dust settle before making decisions.

— CNBC's Stephanie Dhue contributed reporting to this article.

#2763. Ohio State fans want someone to blame. Luke Fahey is the wrong target

Everyone just calm down. You're forcing fury at the wrong person, Buckeye breath.

This mess isn't on Luke Fahey, a freshman quarterback thrown into an untenable situation at Ohio State — and doing enough to win games in one of the two best conferences in college football.

It's on an offensive line that has underachieved all season. It's on an experienced defense with NFL talent that should be seizing control of games, and hasn't.

CFP rankings live predictions: Wake Forest makes statement, Ohio State stays alive

But the low-hanging fruit of frustration is the quarterback, because that's the way it works in football. Too much praise, too much criticism — even after Ohio State's 28-19 win over Northwestern on Saturday.

After Lahey's first win as Ohio State's starting quarterback, merely the most high-profile job in college football. Get in there, kid. We've got games to win.

"This is the first time winning a game with our freshman quarterback, and it's good to build some confidence after the last two weeks," an exasperated Ohio State coach Ryan Day said moments after the Buckeyes snapped a two-game losing streak in front wildly loyal home fans who, at times, weren't having it.

They booed the offense, they booed the defense. They booed the turnovers, they booed the officiating.

But understand this: No. 20 Ohio State isn't out of the College Football Playoff race. There's too much crazy still ahead in November, where teams tighten up amid the pressure, and dreams invariably fade.

Those who don't wilt are those who have been there before, who have seen and dealt with everything — and know how to respond. Which is what makes Ohio State's response to losing starting quarterback Julian Sayin last month so perplexing.

Instead of expecting a three-star freshman quarterback — a developmental recruit who was more depth than instant success — to pull you from the fire, Ohio State should've leaned on the lines of scrimmage to protect Lahey until he grew comfortable and gained confidence.

The offensive line struggled in pass protection in losses to USC and Oregon, and the defensive line failed to dictate tempo and keep Lahey and the offense from chasing points. They both got better against Northwestern, and Lahey continued to play smarter and more efficient.

They ran the offense through All-American wide receiver Jeremiah Smith (17 targets, 11 catches, 117 yards, 1 TD), and the run game had 168 yards — after getting 53 yards last week in a blowout home loss to Oregon. And more than anything, Lahey continued to grow with each repetition.

In a perfect world, the 5-star recruit who has been in the system since early 2025 should be playing quarterback right now. Should be stepping in for the Big Ten's best quarterback, and the offensive regression shouldn't be this obvious.

But there's a reason Tavien St. Clair — a 6-4, 235-pound specimen of a quarterback — isn't playing and Fahey is. Day believes Fahey gives Ohio State its best chance to win games.

And now Fahey is beginning to make plays to reward Day's faith.

Fahey isn't polished, and no way near a finished product. But midway through the fourth quarter in yet another red zone situation, he read pressure, found Smith on a tough throw in the middle of the field — in the middle of traffic — for the game-sealing touchdown.

He's a freshman, he still hasn't seen defensive adjustments that he's getting by the series ― not by the game. Still trying to absorb things he should be learning on the practice field, not during live action against the upper-half of the Big Ten.

He'll have another big moment next week at Nebraska, against another difficult defense and in a loud environment where the Ohio State offensive line needs to help. Control the point of attack, protect, no pre-snap penalties that force long down-and-distance decisions.

Give Fahey every possible chance to help Ohio State win its last two games and hope chaos in front of it leads to the CFP.

"He's just trying to get better," Smith said of Fahey. "He has confidence now. He has to build on it."

Matt Hayes is the senior national college football writer for USA TODAY Sports Network. Follow him on X at @MattHayesCFB. Listen to him daily, from 12-2 p.m., on 1010XL-Jacksonville.
