#2682. Recap: Miami beats Duke 36-25

The Miami Hurricanes started off their home stretch of ACC games on the right foot, defeating former Canes head coach Manny Diaz and his Duke Blue Devils 36-25 on Saturday afternoon at Hard Rock Stadium.

Former Duke QB Darian Mensah continued his Heisman Trophy campaign going 30/41 for 386 yards with a touchdown and no picks. Javian Mallory was an absolute dude, with 150 scrimmage yards and three touchdowns. Cooper Barkate had a huge day with eight catches for 134 yards. Mo Toure had a team-high 11 combined tackles.

Miami and Duke started off slowly on the offensive side of the ball, with the teams trading off five punts between them in the first quarter. Miami opened the scoring with a 39-yard Jake Weinberg field goal early in the second quarter. Duke answered with a field goal 13 plays later. Miami finally found the end zone on a four-yard run by Mark Fletcher, Jr. who left the game with an apparent injury in the first half and did not return. A 40-yard Barkate catch and run was the big play of the drive.

Duke answered on the following drive, and it was the uber-talented Nate Sheppard who broke free for a 47-yard touchdown right up the middle. Sheppard had a field day with 224 scrimmage yards and two scores. Miami would answer with a chip shot field goal shortly before the half for a 13-10 lead at the break.

The Canes got the ball first and drove down the field thanks to a 33-yard run by Jordan Lyle. And it looked like for a second Elija Lofton finally had his nifty end zone catch he was denied last week. But his one-handed grab was made just after he touched out of bounds and was reversed after review and a field goal followed.

Miami forced a punt near midfield, and minutes later, Mallory took a short pass and went 63 yards weaving through traffic and to the end zone for a touchdown and a 22-10 lead. The blocking was nifty on the play from the backfield down the field. And Shannon Dawson made a truly head-scratching call on the two-point conversion attempt with a designed run to Mensah. Mensah was clobbered just before the goal line and bent backwards. You simply can't risk your QB like that.

Duke would answer back five plays later, with Sheppard cutting left and past Miami's defense and getting to the corner on a five-yard run before throwing the U down over his knee (not sure why people do this).

Miami raised that U right back up on the following drive, which was a death march of over seven and a half minutes that took 17 plays and went 79 yards. Mallory tore through the line and across the goal line from two yards for a two-yard score. Three plays later, Xavier Lucas turned for the ball on a poorly thrown pass by Walker Eget, and the Canes secured their only takeaway of the game. Five plays later, Mallory broke free off the left side for a 39-yard touchdown, and church was officially out at 36-17. Duke would add some window dressing with a last second touchdown throw on fourth down with under 30 seconds left to close out the scoring.

A win, and Miami can clinch a spot in the ACC title game if UNC can knock off Louisvile this evening.

#2681. Kyle Shanahan: Mike Evans is getting better, we're trying to make sure he fully heals

The 49ers have ruled out wide receiver Mike Evans for Sunday’s game in Dallas, but head coach Kyle Shanahan says Evans is getting healthy enough to play.

Evans is dealing with Achilles tendinitis and Shanahan said that while Evans’ recovery is progressing and he could probably play if he had to, the 49ers want to prioritize his long-term health and not the short-term benefit of having him on the field on Sunday.

The 33-year-old Evans was off to an outstanding start this season, and he’s the 49ers’ team leader with an average of 70 receiving yards per game. The 49ers want to get that production back, but the top priority is having Evans produce in the playoffs.

29 minutes, 8 points, 10 rebounds, 2 assists, 3 turnovers, 3/8 FG, 0/4 3P, -4

31 minutes, 14 points, 11 rebounds, 3 assists, 2 steals, 4 turnovers, 5 PF, 5/9 FG, 4/7 3P, -3

19 minutes, 3 points, 4 rebounds, 3 assists, 1/4 FG, 1/2 3P, -4

Ament was mostly a help defender against the Magic, and while I thought he was largely fine, he did have a few more moments where he spaced out off the ball; namely, an important possession late where he overhelped on the driver, leaving Trisatn da Silva in the corner, who pumped and drove to the rim for the easy jam.

DNP-CD: Caris LeVert, Bogoljub Markovic, Kasparas Jakucionis, Jericho Sims

#2678. Jerry Jones: "I don't think we're far away" from 18 regular-season games

As the NFL embarks on the second half of its current 18-week regular-season schedule, it’s just a matter of time before the current structure changes.

It’s no secret that the NFL wants to expand the regular season from 17 to 18 games. The league is sufficiently confident about it happening that folks like Cowboys owner Jerry Jones speak of it as a given.

“I don’t think we’re far away from it,” Jones said Friday on 105.3 The Fan in Dallas, regarding the addition of an extra game. “I don’t know how — what is far away. Next month? No. Next year? Maybe. [The] next year? Maybe. That has to be negotiated with the players.

“But it’s in everybody’s best interests.  You’d cut back on the preseason games. You’d have teams more develop in the first few games as the type of thing you were trying to get done in preseason. But it’s in everybody’s interest, and it certainly is in the players’ best interest in my mind, for sure.  And having said that, I would anticipate that coming.”

His comments presume the NFL Players Association will happily agree to 18 regular-season games. They likely won’t. At a minimum, they’ll seek major concessions in exchange for the willingness to add yet another game that counts.

The unspoken goal had been 2027. The NFL delayed picking a date for Super Bowl LXII in Atlanta in order to accommodate the possibility that the game will slide a week or two deeper into February. That would make 2028 the earliest year for expansion, as a practical matter. (Adding a game for 2027 would be possible only if the dead week between the conference championships is wiped out or if the season starts a week earlier. If an 18th game will result in a second bye, both would be required.)

Expansion by 2027 would require expedited negotiations. Expansion by 2028 would hinge on the NFL and NFLPA striking a deal within the next year or so. The union has shown no inclination, however, to engage in talks aimed at extending the current Collective Bargaining Agreement, which runs through the 2030 season.

Still, if push comes to shove, there will be 18 games. The blueprint was created in 2011. The NFL will lock the players out until the players agree to the things the owners want. Most notably, 18 regular-season games and 16 annual international games.

Beyond that, Jones’s comment about the early games of the season is odd. “You’d have teams more develop in the first few games as the type of thing you were trying to get done in preseason.”

He says that as if it’s a good thing. It definitely is not. Already, teams struggle in September to get up to speed, given that most teams (with the exception of those assigned to the Hall of Fame Game) play only three preseason games. When the preseason reduces to two games, that’s even fewer chances to prepare.

It’s also fewer chances for the non-starters to get the attention of coaches and General Managers in games that don’t count in the standings. It will become harder for undrafted free agents to make the 53-man rosters.

Regardless, the motivation isn’t football. It’s money. More inventory equals more weekends equals more broadcast windows equals more revenue.

And that likely will continue until the preseason shrinks to zero games — and the regular season expands to 20 games.

#2676. Charlie Smith throws 3 TD passes and Harvard wraps up fourth straight Ivy championship

PHILADELPHIA (AP) — Charlie Smith threw three touchdown passes, and the Harvard defense held Pennsylvania scoreless in the second half as the Crimson rallied for a 38-24 victory on Saturday, clinching their fourth consecutive Ivy League championship in the process.

Harvard, ranked No. 19 in the Stats Perform FCS Top 25, trailed 24-17 at halftime after surrendering three touchdowns in the final four minutes of the second quarter.

The first of Harvard's three second-half touchdowns came in the middle of the third quarter on Smith's 34-yard pass to Nate Bailey on the first play after a short Penn punt and 11-yard return by Bailey.

After a fourth-down sack by Ethan Carson, the Crimson had another short field, and Xaviah Bascon's 5-yard touchdown run capped off a 34-yard drive for a 31-24 lead.

Kise Flannery's 2-yard touchdown run with 4 1/2 minutes left in the fourth wrapped it up for Harvard (8-1, 5-1 Ivy League).

Harvard leads Princeton and Brown by one game with one game remaining. The Crimson beat both teams earlier in the season.

Smith completed 18 of 28 passes for 199 yards, 113 of which went to Bailey on eight receptions. Bascon rushed for 104 yards on 18 carries.

Karson Siqueiros-Lasky was 15 of 23 passing for 210 yards with a touchdown for Penn (4-6, 2-5).

Smith's 14-yard touchdown pass to Bailey gave the Crimson a 17-3 lead early in the second quarter. Later in the half, Penn scored three touchdowns in the final four minutes on Siqueiros-Lasky's 69-yard touchdown pass to Ronan Johannson, a blocked punt and Zach Darche's 37-yard pick-six.

Harvard has a 56-39-2 lead in the series, first played in 1881.

#2673. Dejounte Murray is available: should the Raptors pay the price?

The case of Dejounte Murray is an interesting one. The Raptors' fanbase seems captivated on two things right now, as the team is experiencing a slump with both Kawhi Leonard and Scottie Barnes out: a new centre, and a new point guard. It seems that one way or another, the people want change. But is Dejounte Murray the right player to bring it?

Murray's history speaks for itself. A defensively minded point guard who could score and facilitate, he was a big part of those pre-Alien San Antonio Spurs teams, before ending up on the New Orleans Pelicans in a mire of injury troubles. For the past few years, Murray has had few opportunities to play basketball, at all, and when he's been on the court, he's not been All-Star he once was.

INGLEWOOD, CA – NOVEMBER 8: Dejounte Murray #5 of the New Orleans Pelicans looks on during the game against the LA Clippers on November 8, 2026 at Intuit Dome in Los Angeles, California. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Juan Ocampo/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

His contract, for a Raptors team that is currently struggling financially, is a breath of fresh air. Making just over $32 million this season, Murray becomes an unrestricted free-agent at the end of the 2027-28 campaign, meaning that he could either be traded, released, or re-signed for a more team-friendly contract, alleviating the Raptors' financial pressures.

Immanuel Quickley, the Raptors' starter at the one, is making $32.5 million until the 2028-29 season, so it would be easy to make the money, and the position, work for the Raptors. Moving off Quickley could allow for Jamal Shead to firmly step into the starting lineup as a pass-first point guard as opposed to Quickley's place as a floor-spacing combo guard, who perhaps plays more naturally at the two. And, if they were to keep Murray, the Raptors would have the flexibility to make big moves and engender what would perhaps be a more stable situation, while retaining the services of a former All-Star. But, is Murray really an upgrade over IQ?

Many complaints have been made about Quickley, but he is also a bonafide volume shooter, something the Raptors desperately need as a part of their offensive schemes. Murray is many things, but he hasn't taken six or more threes per game since 2024. And while Quick is far from an iron man, he played 70 regular season games last year. Again, Murray hasn't done that since… 2024.

On a team with Kawhi Leonard and Jakob Poeltl, there is no sense in getting a third injury-prone starter on the squad, unless the front office is actively trying to tank. And if Murray ends up injured again for the third season in a row, there's no saying what value he'd bring on the trade market. Betting on one players' health is one thing, and betting on that of two is a stretch. But three is just ludicrous, and if you saw your buddy gambling that magnitude in a casino, you'd haul him out of there.

Beyond the on-court realities, Dejounte Murray is someone who actively disrespected Jamal Shead last season, someone who is an increasingly important part of this Raptors' team. That situation, where Murray dropped Shead and got up in his face after hitting the shot, was ugly as sin. Immanuel Quickley ran up to Murray to stick up for his teammate, and the whole thing just puts a bad taste in my mouth regarding what a trade for the point guard would look like.

Frankly, I'm all for aggressiveness and competitiveness, but considering that Murray and Shead didn't have any sort of known rivalry, this move was just disrespectful. Bringing that energy into the Raps' locker room doesn't seem to be the right move when this team's success seems so heavily predicated on good chemistry.

The reality for the Raptors is that unless their starters' health and production stay unrealistically consistent, they may very well have to make a trade to get this team looking right in the postseason. But, there's no sense in making moves, just for the sake of making moves.

Trying to clear cap space is likely going to be a need, but doing that without a clear plan is not worth it, especially if it results in sacrificing one of Toronto's best options for floor spacing, which its starting lineup already struggles with. Clearly, based on this summer, the front office is willing and able to wait for good deals to come by, and there are very few worlds in which a deal for Dejounte Murray is a good one for Toronto.

#2672. Ground stop results in side judge Don Willard serving as referee for two games on Sunday

Friday’s nationwide ground stop won’t keep NFL teams from getting to their road games on Sunday. It will, however, impact the ability of officials to get to where they need to be.

The NFL has announced that officiating assignments have changed for Week 10. And the situation will result in a backup referee serving as the referee in two games on the same day.

“Due to the ongoing nationwide impact to air travel this weekend, the NFL has adjusted its officiating assignments for Week 10 games, reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns,” the NFL said in a statement. “The changes will necessitate that three backup referees — umpires Barry Anderson and Duane Heydt and side judge Don Willard [pictured] — will work as referees in the following games: Carolina-New Orleans – Duane Heydt; Jacksonville-Tennessee – Barry Anderson; Miami-Indianapolis and Pittsburgh-Cincinnati – Don Willard.

“Each of the league’s 17 officiating crews have a backup referee identified, and that individual trains throughout the year to work at the referee position should the need arise.”

The situation creates the likely unprecedented situation of a referee working two games in one day. Willard will handle Dolphins-Colts at 1:00 p.m. ET, and then he’ll make the 109-mile trip from Indianapolis to Cincinnati for the Sunday night game.

Making the unprecedented even more unusual is the fact that Willard’s usual crew (led by referee Scott Novak) wasn’t scheduled to work at all this weekend.

The announcement doesn’t address where the referees for those three games will be working, or what their roles will be. Shawn Smith was scheduled to be the referee for Panthers-Saints, Alex Moore was set to be the referee for Jaguars-Titans, Carl Cheffers was due to be the referee for Dolphins-Colts, and Clete Blakeman was slated to be the referee for Steelers-Bengals.

The league’s statement also doesn’t specify other shifts that were required as to the established crews that work together throughout the regular season.

#2669. Report: Vikings first reached out to Raiders about Kirk Cousins on "midday Monday"

As it turns out, the Vikings contacted the Raiders about a possible trade for quarterback Kirk Cousins before Monday night’s meltdown from quarterback Carson Wentz.

Via ESPNFL, the Vikings initially contacted the Raiders during “midday Monday,” prior to Minnesota’s Week 9 game against the Bills. The Vikings told the Raiders they wanted to see how things went during the Monday night game before having any further conversations.

Then came Wentz’s 8.9-passer rating performance in a 23-6 loss, and Minnesota mobilized. The Vikings, per the report, contacted the Raiders before 6:00 a.m. PT on Tuesday and commenced the talks that culminated in a deal being done.

Said Raiders G.M. John Spytek during a Tuesday press conference: “I never made one call on Kirk Cousins. And I got a few phone calls. But one real one this morning.”

The Vikings initially offered a fifth-round pick for Cousins, per the report. The report doesn’t specify the Raiders’ opening position.

Once the Vikings moved to a third-round pick, the Raiders pounced.

Beyond avoiding the $10 million guaranteed bonus and clearing the path for rookie No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza (which are mentioned in the article), the Raiders ultimately bought a third-round pick for $650,000 (which is not).

That’s the most attractive aspect of the entire transaction, in our view. Nearly 10 years ago, the Browns bought a second-round pick from the Texans by assuming quarterback Brock Osweiler’s $16 million full guarantee for the 2017 season. Any team would sprint for the chance to purchase a third-round pick in the 2027 draft for only $650,000.

In this case, that bargain came with nine starts from Cousins, four wins, and months of excellent mentorship for Mendoza.

As to the lingering sense in some circles that the Raiders could have gotten even more for Cousins, they risked driving a bargain so hard that the Vikings would have walked away and made a trade with another team.

So it was a win for the Vikings, who got their first choice. It was a win for the Raiders. And it definitely was a win for Cousins, who went from waiting to be benched for Mendoza to having nine games as the starter for a contender — plus the strong possibility that the Vikings will make the playoffs.

The Rockets did allow the Jazz to shoot 46 percent, but they ultimately pulled off the win to move to 10-3 on the season.

The Jazz were led by Darryn Peterson with 28 points, Keyonte George with 27 and Ace Bailey with 21.

The Rockets are off tonight, but they will return to action on Sunday, where they will kick off a back-to-back set with a matchup against the Washington Wizards, rolling into another road game against the Miami Heat on Monday.

#2664. Grading quarterback Jared Curtis after Vanderbilt football loss to Alabama

Vanderbilt football lost to Alabama 21-6 at FirstBank Stadium on Nov. 14, failing to score a touchdown for the first time this season.

The Commodores (2-6, 1-6 SEC) played well defensively, but the offense had only 39 rushing yards (not including sacks) and the team committed 14 penalties for 92 yards. Freshman quarterback Jared Curtis had to produce most of the offensive yards himself.

All six points came on a pair of 50-plus yard field goals from Brock Taylor.

Curtis was 25-for-40 passing for 223 yards. He didn't throw any touchdowns or commit any turnovers.

He was sacked five times for 27 yards. He ran four times for 9 yards.

Curtis had an uneven performance against Alabama. On one hand, he didn't commit any turnovers, something that hurt him against Kentucky and Arkansas. However, his efficiency wasn't what it was in some of the earlier games.

He made only one throw of more than 20 yards, missed some open receivers and sometimes completed throws that didn't gain much yardage. He also threw out of the end zone on fourth-and-4, down two touchdowns, when any attempt to make a play would've been better than throwing it away.

Curtis didn't lose Vanderbilt the game − the bigger issues were penalties and an inability to run the ball − but he didn't do anything to win it, either.

#2661. Badgers embarrassed by Maryland for second straight year

The Wisconsin Badgers suffered an embarrassing 24-21 loss to the Maryland Terrapins for the second year in a row, once again raising questions about Luke Fickell and the direction of the program after the 31-10 win over Rutgers last weekend.

Wisconsin entered the week on a strong note, as they had dominated Rutgers in true freshman quarterback Ryan Hopkins's first start last weekend. They came into the game as 8.5-point favorites and were still in the mix in the Big Ten race with a 6-3 record and 4-2 conference record.

However, just like last weekend, the Badgers suffered a surprising loss. A season ago, Wisconsin was embarrassed 27-10 on their own home field, which sparked a six-game losing streak. This season, it was a 24-21 loss to one of the worst teams in the Big Ten this season.

Wisconsin opened the game on a high note, forcing a quick three-and-out on the first set of plays, while responding with a five-play, 57-yard touchdown drive. The Badgers got great field position and took advantage with a 21-yard Jaylon Domingeaux catch, a pass interference call, and a 17-yard Darrion Dupree run, leading to a four-yard touchdown run on the next play.

The Badgers allowed one first down on their next set of plays, but quickly forced a punt again and seemed to be picking up where they left off a week ago. But on 4th & 1 at their own 39-yard line, they decided to go for it with a fullback dive, and Ryan Schwendeman fumbled. Clearly, the Badgers didn't feel like a quarterback sneak was an option, and there was the lane to convert, but the fumble gave Maryland great field position.

Credit goes to the defense, though, who got help from the Terrapins with two false starts to force a quick three-and-out and get the ball back on a punt, albeit at Wisconsin's own 1-yard line. The Badgers went to Bryan Jackson twice, getting nothing, before a short pass on fourth down forced them to punt deep in their own territory.

Once again, Maryland got great field position, even with a penalty at the end of the punt, starting at their own 47-yard line. But the defense was stellar again, as it had been throughout the first quarter, and Maryland opened the second quarter with a missed 51-yard field goal.

Finally, the offense got some rhythm. Abu Sama, who was nowhere to be found in the first quarter, ripped an 18-yard run on his first touch, and Darrion Dupree followed that up with eight and 11-yard runs later in the drive to set up two more first downs. The Badgers got themselves in the red zone, but what has killed them all season hurt them again: a negative play on first down. That ended up derailing the drive, and they were forced to settle for a field goal.

Midway through the second quarter, the defense had their worst drive of the game so far. Without a pass rush affecting the quarterback, Cardell Williams ripped off six straight completions before a quarterback keeper for one yard ended up in the end zone. Suddenly, a game where the Badgers defense had dominated through the first 20+ minutes was 10-7 with three minutes left in the half.

Wisconsin went nowhere on its next drive, as Sama got just two yards before an incompletion and a sack on second and third down. So, the Badgers quickly punted, and Maryland got a great opportunity to tie the game up before halftime.

Once again, it was a ton of Cardell Williams, both with his arms and his legs, as Maryland's backup quarterback moved the ball down the field in the two-minute drill. Starting at Wisconsin's 40-yard line, the Terrapins had four rushes and two passes, getting all the way down to the one-yard line. But Matt Jung and Mason Posa forced a huge fumble on a one-yard carry, recovering the ball before halftime and saving a touchdown. Unfortunately, Jung was carted off with a leg injury, needing a cast on his foot.

The Badgers started with the ball in the second half, but their offense remained lifeless with another three-and-out, starting with a negative play. It really felt at this point that Jeff Grimes had no faith in his quarterback. The Badgers went screen (for -1), run (for five), and screen (for -2) for a three-and-out.

The defense bounced back from two shaky drives with a quick three-and-out, but the Badgers coughed it up immediately. After a first down drop, Darrion Dupree took the second-down handoff and fumbled after no gain, with Maryland recovering and returning it to the Wisconsin 16-yard line.

Four runs later, the Terrapins were in the end zone with a surprise 14-13 lead. Now, there was still a ton of ball game left, but Wisconsin's offense looked shattered, and they needed a turnaround fast with injuries piling up on the defensive side.

And it didn't look good at first. The Badgers got no gain on first down, one yard on a second-down screen, and nothing on third down for a quick three-and-out. But Sean West was roughed on the punt, giving Wisconsin a free 15 yards. That, plus an unsportsmanlike conduct, took the Badgers from their own 31 to the Maryland 39.

From there, Wisconsin went with five straight dropbacks, completing just one for 15 yards, which set up an easier field goal for Gavin Lahm from 41 yards, cutting the lead to 14-13.

Maryland's next drive was instantly killed by a false start and a holding penalty on the first two plays, and they quickly punted, with the Badgers getting the ball at their own 43-yard line.

Well, Wisconsin finally started to get a rhythm and consistently move the ball, with Ryan Hopkins having a couple of nice scrambles and Jeff Grimes mixing in an end around. The Badgers quickly moved into the red zone after a 28-yard Hopkins run and, two plays later, punched it in from the one-yard line for a Darrion Dupree touchdown.

Despite how poorly their offense had played, the Badgers were back on top, and they went for two to make it 21-14 at the top of the fourth quarter.

Maryland's offense was able to move a bit on its next drive, thanks to a 13-yard run from DeJuan Williams on 4th & 1 and a 15-yard penalty on backup safety Matthew Traynor, but its own holding penalty killed a very promising drive, as they punted in plus territory once again.

With 8:43 left, the Badgers started with the ball on their own 10-yard line. This felt like the perfect time for them to kill clock and start to move the ball a bit offensively. They didn't get a single yard, punting in less than a minute, and Maryland was in position to tie things up with 7:45 left.

Well, penalties were the Terrapins' Achilles ' heel. As their run game started to get going and they advanced to the Wisconsin 35-yard line, another unsportsmanlike conduct penalty came. Maryland didn't recover and, once again, punted in plus territory.

With 4:29 left on their own 20-yard line, could this be the drive for the Badgers to seal the deal? Darrion Dupree got five on the first play, but was stuffed on 2nd & 5. Then Ryan Hopkins fumbled a third-down snap, sending the Badgers back and forcing their fifth three-and-out of the game. Sean West's punt went just 35 yards to midfield, which the Terrapins returned to the Wisconsin 39.

One play later, the score was tied, as Cardell Williams hit Preston Howard for a 39-yard catch-and-run touchdown. Wisconsin had a ton of opportunities to close the game, and they never capitalized. But the game wasn't over, as the Badgers had the ball with 2:11 left and all their timeouts.

Things started great as Darrion Dupree took a screen 15 yards to get the Badgers a 1st & 10 at their own 40 at the 2-minute warning. Well, disaster struck after that, as Ryan Hopkins didn't identify a free rusher and was crushed by the blitzer, fumbling and getting hurt in the process.

So Maryland had the ball on the Wisconsin 33-yard line, needing just a field goal to take the lead. They ran the ball six times, getting one first down before kicking a field goal on 4th & 1 at Wisconsin's 12, securing the 24-21 lead.

The Badgers had just 29 seconds left with no timeouts and Colton Joseph in the game off the bench. Joseph committed an illegal forward pass on his first play, essentially sealing the game for the Badgers, and Wisconsin would go on to suffer its fourth loss of the season.

This was an ugly one for the Badgers. The offense compiled just 201 total yards, going 2 of 12 on third downs, as Ryan Hopkins had a rough day, averaging 3.5 yards per pass. They also committed three turnovers, gifting Maryland some great field position.

Defensively, the Badgers played well enough to win. They stopped the run, and the Terrapins went 2 of 13 on third downs. But they allowed Cardell Williams to get too comfortable in the pocket, marking the third time this year they've done that to a backup quarterback (Iowa, UCLA).

This is an embarrassing loss for the Badgers and one that requires some deep thinking about the direction of the program, given how inconsistent this team has been over the past few weeks.

Instead, the Clippers captured their first NBA Cup group play victory, surviving a 113-112 thriller and handing the Thunder their third consecutive loss.

The Indiana Pacers secured their first NBA Cup win in dramatic fashion, edging out the defending champions, the New York Knicks, in a 106-104 contest. Pascal Siakam led the Pacers with 19 points, while Aaron Nesmith added 18 points to seal their victory and improve their record to 1-1 in group play.

#2655. NFL predictions: In Browns-Texans, Cleveland needs to turn the corner to become a serious threat

This Sunday, the Cleveland Browns (5-4) take on the Houston Texans (3-5). Below, we analyze a few advantages, disadvantages, or general thoughts about the two teams before getting to our predictions for the game.

The start to the season for the Cleveland Browns was a feel-good story. Todd Monken in his first year as a head coach, all of the young players shining at times, and Deshaun Watson having five game-winning drives. And it was fun to harp on the incredible stat of all of those victories having game-winning drives, but we all know that isn't sustainable. If the Browns want to contend for the postseason the rest of the year, something has to change.

Playing every winnable game down-to-the-wire hasn't gone away.

The run game issues on both sides haven't gone away.

I praised Todd Monken and Mike Rutenberg earlier this season for their ability to adapt and make adjustments. I don't think that has stalled, I think what we're seeing now are the true weaknesses of this team, and they aren't marks of a playoff contender. Cleveland's hopes seem to rest on taking advantage of their easy schedule, but they've blown their margin for error in that category too with losses to the Jets and Saints.

I think the coaching staff is trying to get it fixed each week, but so far they've mostly come up empty. That doesn't mean the team can't turn the corner in some of those areas, but the thing I keep saying now is, "this is the team's four-game home stretch." I don't necessarily expect them to win all four games, which would put them at a ridiculous 7-0 at home, but on a game-by-game basis, we need to see this team pull of a dominant performance somewhere. Something to further bolster their confidence, further establish their identity, and to ride for the rest of the season.

As a follow-up to the above, there is one X-factor who could, at any point, make a monumental difference to the team. Let's get into it with some of our miscellaneous notes this week:

That X-factor would be……….DE Jared Verse. It's been a storyline all season — he was brought here, not to replicate what Myles Garrett did, but to be a damn-good alternative to him, at least when it comes to pressuring the quarterback. Overall, despite the run defense woes, the Browns' defense has been fairly solid this season, and the sacks are coming from everywhere but the edge. If Cleveland's defense is doing this good with Verse being a non-factor, or dare I say it, a liability, what is the upside to this unit if the switch finally flips for him?

We've hated on Verse a lot, but this week, he finally admitted that he hasn't played to the standard he wants, and that he's talked to the team's psychiatrist about it. I'm a firm believer in how the mental aspects of things can screw with your game. We see it most obviously with kickers all the time. Sometimes we see it with receivers and their drops. I thought Deshaun Watson had a mental block the past several years that he finally seems to have cleared. It's possible it's there with Verse. Verse says it's not physical, so something has to explain the extreme dropoff of being one of the league's best to one of the league's worst performing players. Maybe this is a step to somewhat tackling whatever is getting in the way of him being the player he's proven he can be. If he can deliver that against the Texans, maybe it's the boost that Cleveland needs to put away a game.

That presents us with the unique challenge of trying to figure out which Houston Texans team we'll see. C.J. Stroud has been a bit of a disappointment the past few years, and last year, the team went on an incredible stretch to close out the year due to their defense. This season, I feel like the defense has been crap, and Stroud is lighting it up most weeks. But this defense should be better; they've often been plagued by giving up big plays in pass defense.

Cleveland's pass defense needs to be up to the challenge this week. Although some teams have used the run lately to combat the Browns, I feel like Houston won't be so committed to the ground game.

Deshaun Watson starting over Shedeur Sanders this week is probably the right call. As much as I enjoyed Sanders finally letting loose in the fourth quarter and overtime last week, many of those plays aren't sustainable. When it was time to read-and-react in the first several quarters, things were too slow still, the operation was off, etc. The offense has had similar slow starts with Watson, of course, but the operation for the most part has been smooth with him.

According to FanDuel, the Browns are 4.5 point underdogs against the Texans. The over/under is 40.5.

Offensive coordinator Travis Switzer talked about how the team has tried to work on ways to start faster offensively:

"Yeah, the first thing as a staff, we looked at everything that we've done early in games, and when we looked at it, it was like, man, we've kind of tried a little bit of everything as far as, hey, let's maybe call some can plays early, or we've tried running it early. We've tried movement passes. So, we looked at that, and nothing really spiked out as far as, hey, this is the direction we should go there. And then we've also just stressed it to the guys, especially early in practice, like Wednesdays, the first period is always a tempo period, the first team period, so we've tried to stress it there. It's like, okay, we're going fast, but also, hey, we're trying to start fast. That's the point of this period here. And yeah, I can't say that it's been like one thing that jumped out to us. We just got to keep attacking it and try to stress it and just try to get better there."

Defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg was asked about Jared Verse's admission that he's seen the team psychiatrist to try to be a better pass rusher:

"I'm not going to discuss Jared Verse in terms of what he does off the field, but I'm really proud of Jared for his approach, for his attitude, the way he's working with his teammates and our D-line coaching staff to help himself get to where he wants to go."

Special teams coordinator Bryon Storer was asked about gunners when they run out of bounds (as Cleveland did last week):

"All right, so when you're putting the ball, you're putting it toward – usually you're trying to punt it toward the boundary to shorten the field. And so, you have releases by the gunners toward the punt direction. So, you'd like for both your gunners to release the same direction. So, if you're punting left, both guys release left, and one guy ends up into the boundary. Now, you can't run out of bounds on your own. A lot of times those corners will force you into the white. And so now you have to, take a line to re-enter. You know, what happened on that play was, DT (Daniel Thomas) didn't realize he had gotten in the white, and so we just had a discussion on the sideline and just said, 'hey, if there's any possibility that you could have gone out of bounds, all you got to do is just point to the ball, tell your teammates, you, you, you, and they touch it.' So, it's a big learning experience for us, and unfortunately, it cost us 30 yards of field position, so we had to learn the hard way. But I just don't think that it's possible to change what we do in terms of staying out of bounds. That's just part of the deal."

Here are predictions from multiple staff members at DBN:

Chris Pokorny: "The Browns have played a lot of close games, and are 3-0 at home, so this four-game home stretch that they are beginning is vital for them to stay in the playoff race. The Browns' pass defense has remained a strong suit, but offensively, they still have some consistency issues, with too many dry stretches of scoring. Of all the games the Browns have played this season, this is the one where I feel like I have no idea what to expect. C.J. Stroud seems to be playing at an unexpectedly high level, but the Browns' pass defense has been solid. Will Houston commit to the run, which Cleveland hasn't been able to stop for weeks? And while Houston's defense has struggled compared to my expectations, the talent seems to still be there, so do they get back on track against their former quarterback who takes a lot of sacks?" Browns 24, Texans 21

Jared Mueller: "The Browns are 3-0 at home, are coming off two straight losses, and Deshaun Watson takes back over at quarterback after a one-week concussion-related hiatus. The Texans have not been that good this year but have regrouped a bit and could have a healthy defense on the road in Cleveland.

For some reason, Jared Verse's admission of flaws is a confidence builder for me, despite Houston's talented offense." Browns 27, Texans 24

Thomas Moore: "I don't even know what to make of this team anymore. They win when it seems like all hope is lost, but then lose to the likes of the Jets and the Saints. The Texans will present a challenge, especially with their pass rush, but it's hard to know how good they are, either, because two of their three wins have come against the Titans and Chargers. The thought of the Browns going into the bye week on a three-game losing streak and having everyone bleat for the next two weeks about a quarterback change is too much to even consider." Browns 17, Texans 14

Barry Shuck: "Before the season began, I believed that the Texans would be one of the four best teams in the AFC. I also choose the wrong women. And although Houston might not make the playoffs, they have won three of their last four games and scored 44 points last weekend. The Texans have a prolific passing attack and the Browns are ranked #13 against the pass, so that will be a good chess match. They can't run the ball, but neither can the Browns. Cleveland is middle of the pack in their passing game while Houston is listed in the lower third defending the pass. So, maybe the Browns can air it out to Harold Fannin and either of their two rookie receivers. Defense, or lack of, will be the determining factor. Cleveland will need to find ways to finish drives. Thank goodness for a good kicker and punter." Texans 27, Browns 20

Ezweav: "We're definitely hitting the rough patch. It's a little promising watching the A22 against the Saints and seeing so many wide open plays (mostly missed) but the Texans aren't the Saints so it'll probably be a tougher slog

Defense should hold their own but CJ Stroud is a real quarterback so I don't love the matchup.  We'll probably be talking about how 5-5 still exceeds preseason expectations tomorrow afternoon." Texans 23, Browns 19

Curtiss Brown: "This game will be about as close of a playoff type game as can be. Considering what's at stake, it should be. The Houston Texans have been one of the bigger disappointments this season. As talented as the Texans defense is, they haven't been nearly as dominant. The Texans defense isn't really special in terms of scheme but the talent is there. The run defense is somewhat leaky and they are suspect to give up explosive plays in the passing game.

Houston's offense is starting to click a bit. Quarterback CJ Stroud might force the Texans to back up the Brinks truck if he finds a way to keep up this play. Houston will be down a couple of key defensive players so the Browns must take advantage of it.

Wouldn't surprise me if Cleveland stunned Houston but I dont see that happening." Texans 30, Browns 24 (OT)

On the decision to draw up the final shot for Karl-Anthony Towns instead of Jalen Brunson:

"I don't know if we fouled that much, but we were fouling. They just could keep putting their head down and driving into us, and we weren't ready to play. On the Knicks' inconsistent offensive rhythm and the need to improve:

On missing the potential game-tying shot against Indiana:

On taking full responsibility for his struggles and needing to improve:

"When times are tough, you just gotta own up to it and just be better.

On the Knicks' crowded wing rotation and the possibility of roster changes:

On his shooting struggles and the impact of missing several weeks of basketball activity:

On his mental struggles following the loss to Indiana:

"Just have to be better. Have to be better mentally. I just gotta get my mental right."

On not knowing how to improve his mental state and on-court performance:

"Wish I could tell you. Don't know. … I gotta figure out how to improve that and improve my play."

On why he has struggled to finish shots around the rim:

"It's early. We're not where we wanna be, but it's November. Everything needs to be better."

On the need for staying ready and responding to adversity:

"You're playing well one day and [then] next time you get punched in the mouth. So it's always about how you respond in this league."

#2651. Salem football's 'Blue Storm' rolls to sectional title victory

PAULSBORO – Antonio Merendino says every time the Salem High School football team takes the field, it feels like an event.

The Rams have become a huge hit in the postseason and, on Saturday, earned some well-deserved hardware for their performance.

Salem raced to an 18-point lead in the first half and cruised to a 38-14 victory at Paulsboro in Saturday's Central Jersey Group 1 championship game, earning the program's first sectional title since 2022.

More: Everything you need to know for the 2026 high school football season

The Rams (9-3) will play at South Jersey champion Schalick (12-0) in Friday's state semifinal. The winner will play in the state Group 1 final at MetLife Stadium in the Meadowlands the final weekend of November.

"It feels so surreal right now," said Merendino, a defensive lineman who led a stout defense with two sacks. "It looked so rough in the beginning of the season, but we stuck together and this win shows us that the path to a state championship is right in front of us now."

The squad, which calls itself the Blue Storm, weathered some rough seas over the first four weeks of the season that resulted in a 1-3 start. Included in the bumpy stretch was an 8-6 loss to Paulsboro and a 15-14 setback to Schalick, two games that Salem held leads late in the game.

While Salem got some key players into its lineup following the Schalick loss, Merendino points to something else that helped guide the team through the tough start.

"Coach Carr is the code," Merendino said about Salem head coach Kemp Carr. "That man brought us here, he has shown us the way to win. We know what it takes and how to win now.

"It feels like every single game is an event and we're always chasing for something new. We're the Blue Storm, we're coming for it all."

After head coaching stints at Penns Grove and Winslow, Carr returned to his alma mater in 2024. The team went 0-9 that season.

"I've never had a fast pace anywhere I've gone, I've never had the cabinets full," Carr said. "I've always had to build a program. Sometimes it takes time."

Along with the sectional championship trophy, Carr celebrated his 100th career victory, becoming the first coach in South Jersey history to reach the century mark in both basketball and football, according to local historian Chuck Langerman. Carr went 137-68 as Penns Grove's hoops coach while earning 74 wins at the football coach there. He went 11-18 during his stretch at Winslow and is now 15-17 at Salem.

Carr didn't spend much time talking about the milestone, but instead talked about the city he came from.

"It's all about the community," Carr said. "We made this pack and commitment to each other, we wanted to do it for the community. You get a lot of energy from those people, we don't have a lot there, but one thing we do have is football.

"There are really good people there too. We wanted to make sure we didn't let the community down. We didn't want to let the school down."

Salem has become a must-see event over the last two months, winning eight consecutive games and outscoring the opposition 318-53 over the stretch including 114-14 in three postseason contests.

Salem's game plan was pretty simple: Pound the football right at Paulsboro.

The Rams racked up 325 yards on the ground as sophomore Cashmir Parsley ran for 196 yards and three touchdowns while senior quarterback Desmund Thomas added 105 yards. Thomas only attempted two pass plays in the game – completing both for 14 yards.

Parsley has eclipsed the 100-rushing yard mark 10 times this season, including each of the last seven games. He has 1,500 yards for the season to go along with 19 touchdowns.

"He's so special and young too," Carr said about his workhorse running back. "He's just learning how to tote the rock."

Salem's defense was just as productive. Led by a defensive line of Merendino, Myshon Barnes, Raymond Brown and Isiah Carn, the Rams held Paulsboro to 15 rushing yards, recorded four sacks and two takeaways. Kane Green had an interception to close out the first half while David Harris pounced on a fumble on Paulsboro's second-half kickoff return.

Merendino has at least one sack in 11 straight games and has 18.5 for the season.

Salem sophomore Ahmad Tucker returned a punt 45 yards for a touchdown, but was ejected later in the game. He will have to sit out the state semifinal game because of NJSIAA disqualification rules.

Paulsboro finished its season at 9-3. Junior quarterback Jahsir Johnson threw for 174 yards and a touchdown to Julian Gaines. Jeremiah Carr accounted for the Red Raiders' other TD with a 1-yard run.

#2648. Packers, Broncos explored possible Tony Pollard trade

One week before the trade deadline, teams had interest in Titans running back Tony Pollard. But Tennessee was not yet talking.

The Titans eventually engaged, but no one met their price.

Via ESPNFL, the Packers and Broncos “checked in” on Pollard. The Titans wouldn’t move Pollard for less than a third-round pick.

Both teams had been linked to Colts running back Jonathan Taylor. The Colts, after creating the impression that Taylor would be traded, opted to take the best offer they could get.

The fact that Green Bay and Denver explored acquiring two different tailbacks isn’t much of a vote of confidence in their current depth charts. As to the Packers, it underscores the potentially tenuous status of Josh Jacobs.

Pollard, a fourth-round pick of the Cowboys in 2019, started his career as the backup/understudy to Ezekiel Elliott. Pollard had a breakthrough season in 2022, rushing for 1,007 yards and making it to the Pro Bowl despite Elliott still being the starter. (Elliott gained 876 yards that season.)

Pollard became the full-time starter in 2023, a franchise-tag season. He signed with the Titans in 2024.

He has four straight 1,000-yard seasons. Through eight games in 2026, he has 595 yards. Which puts him on pace for what would be a career-high 1,190 yards.

Pollard is in the final year of a three-year, $21.75 million contract. He’s due to be a free agent in March.

#2644. Justin Allgaier Says Deciding to Retire Took the Pressure Off in His Title Season

Justin Allgaier says deciding 2026 would be his last NASCAR O'Reilly Auto Parts Series season took the pressure off and made his second title year the most fun of his career.

Allgaier explained it to Will Buxton on SPEED with Harvick and Buxton, in a clip shared by SPEED on FOX.

"I can assure you, a thousand percent, you are on the nail on the head. When I decided I was quitting, it made me realize why I love the sport way more," Allgaier said.

"You get so caught up in the day-to-day and wanting simulator time and study time and being in the gym and doing all these things. When I said I was retiring, it took a pressure off of my shoulders that I was like, this is the best thing that's ever happened to my career," he said.

Allgaier told JR Motorsports in December 2025 that he would step away after the season. He and his family had bought a home in Illinois, and the plan included possibly taking over the family business, D&M Speed Shop, one day.

He said the people around him noticed the difference.

"And everybody kept saying, hey, I don't understand. You do realize you have a championship to go win this weekend, right? Like, you were not nervous. You just seem free," Allgaier said.

"I'm like, yeah, I mean, I was retiring. This is money in the bank. This is house money right here. So I get to go have fun and enjoy it. And I think that that's been the catalyst for what's made this year so much fun," he said.

The change also coincided with a career year. Allgaier won six regular-season races, a career best, and entered the Chase as the top seed.

His title run was not smooth. Trouble at Gateway and a crash at Las Vegas briefly dropped him behind Sheldon Creed in the standings.

He recovered with top-five finishes at Charlotte, Phoenix, Talladega and Martinsville. He went to Homestead-Miami Speedway with a 22-point lead over Jesse Love.

Allgaier finished seventh and clinched his second title in three seasons. It was the fifth drivers' championship for JR Motorsports, which Dale Earnhardt Jr. co-owns with his sister, Kelley Earnhardt Miller, and Rick Hendrick.

By then, the retirement plan had changed. Allgaier said in May that his plans were no longer certain, and he later signed a multiyear deal to stay in the No. 7 Chevrolet.

Kelley Earnhardt Miller has also weighed in on the extension. Earnhardt Jr., meanwhile, said this week that he wanted to tell Allgaier to calm down during the finale but worried about a penalty.

The 40-year-old will chase a third O'Reilly Series title in 2027. This time, he will not be racing as if every week is his last in racing, a mindset he credits for making 2026 so much fun.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2639. Hawks unable to outlast Bulls in overtime loss

The Atlanta Hawks were in action in the NBA Cup on Friday night but came up short in a 125-117 road loss in overtime against the Chicago Bulls. Jalen Johnson registered a triple-double of 27 points, 11 rebounds, and 10 assists and CJ McCollum added 20 points off the bench. For the Bulls — without star rookie Caleb Wilson — Norman Powell led the way with 33 points with seven Bulls scoring in double-digits.

The Hawks would have entered this game as favorites, with the Bulls heading into this game on the back of an eight-game losing streak and looking for just their second win of the season. Without impressive rookie Caleb Wilson, the Bulls were missing talent that is sorely needed and handed the Hawks a significant advantage with his absence. In reality, that is not how it played out.

The Hawks' time spent leading this game was extremely brief, and it was the Bulls who ran out to a double-digit lead in the first quarter behind 10 first quarter points from Powell. The key difference in this game began to become clear from the first quarter as the Hawks shot 2-of-8 from three-point range as the visitors' struggles shooting the ball became more concrete in the second quarter. The Bulls, meanwhile, had no problem dispatching their three-pointers and began to run their lead to a game-high 18 points in the second quarter.

While the Hawks found some success in the paint — and this was how they began to reign in the Chicago lead — the three-point shooting story was becoming clear: 3-of-17 for Atlanta, while the Bulls shot 11-of-28 from three in the first half. The Hawks were, at times, settling for transition, pull-up threes from above the break but only shot 1-of-11 from such shots in this game:

Off of a miss, Nickeil Alexander-Walker pushes the ball up the floor and springs into a three-pointer, but cannot convert:

Off of the pass from Dyson Daniels, Johnson pulls up into a three-pointer which is missed:

On this attempt, the Hawks work themselves into a better opportunity from above the break, with Alexander-Walker finding Daniels, who finds Onyeka Okongwu all alone above the break, but the three is missed:

The Hawks would continue to strike out on these opportunities all night long, and relied on the inside scoring of Johnson, and some tough, crafty baskets from McCollum to keep the visitors in range, even tying the game in late stages of the third quarter.

The Bulls, however, quickly stretched their lead back to 10 in the fourth quarter, giving the Hawks a lot of work to do on the road. Even with 2:22 remaining the Hawks faced an uphill battle of seven points, but Okongwu and Johnson, tied the game.

Having not led the game since the first quarter — when the game was 7-6 — the Hawks had multiple opportunities to take a late lead in this game. The first comes in the form of the Hawks failing to secure a rebound off of a missed shot from Jalen Smith, with Johnson losing the rebound and the Bulls get the opportunity to call a timeout:

After a missed shot from Powell inside, the Hawks get a chance to get out in transition. Johnson is faced by Josh Giddey, and elects to pass the ball back out to the perimeter to Alexander-Walker, who is unable to hit the three-pointer:

I'm not sure Johnson realized how strong his advantage was here: no help was coming, Giddey was on his own, and it's a one-on-one near the rim you would heavily back Johnson to score or draw a foul. Instead, he makes the unselfish play and finds Alexander-Walker, who continued his unfortunate shooting trend in this game at the wrong time.

The Hawks would get another chance as they advance the ball off of a timeout after another Bulls miss. Okongwu delivers a good pass to the cutting Aaron Wiggins, who is surely rim-side and through for a layup, but cannot complete the catch as the ball slips through his fingers and out of play:

Three differing chances for the Hawks to get/to score and all of them passed them by, and the game goes to overtime.

The Hawks would take their first lead since the first quarter, but it would not last, as Powell scored nine points in the overtime period to pull away from the Hawks before a dagger three Matas Buzelis dashes any hopes of a Hawks victory.

Postgame, Hawks head coach Quin Snyder highlighted the start of the game as an issue for the Hawks and discussed how the Hawks' shooting issues were exacerbated by the Bulls' own good three-point shooting night.

"We didn't play with the force at the beginning of the game," said Snyder postgame. "That impacts our defense, it's, kind of, the complimentary of basketball: how your defense affects your offense. When we're not forceful defensively, or active, and we're not running. We know the things we need to have in the front of our minds to focus on. When we don't do that, we don't play well. By the same token, we started to find that, 18 (points) down. When you're not shooting the ball well — we had a bad shooting night, which is going to happen — those things become even more important. When your opponent is shooting the ball, it compounds itself. We take from it what we can, and there's a lot here we can focus on."

"We've got to come out with energy from the jump, we just didn't do that," added Jalen Johnson.

This game can be summed up by living by the three and dying by the three. The Hawks finished with 8-of-40 from three (20%) while the Bulls shot 20-of-50 from three (40%), and while there are other nuances of this game that did not go the Hawks' way (which we'll touch on in a moment), the game can really be summed up as simply as that. If you hit eight threes while your opponent hits 20 (a 60-24 point disparity) it's difficult to win games consistently. The fact the Hawks almost did, speaks to the nature of the Bulls' season (allowing Jalen Smith to 15 shots and 1-of-6 from three is something the Bulls allowed to happen, for some reason).

From the Hawks' side, it was another difficult night shooting the three from Alexander-Walker, who shot 1-of-11 from three, and 6-of-19 from the field — it just wasn't his night, and there's been a couple of those this season where it becomes evident it may not be his night from three and he ends up with a poor percentage on a high volume. It was the same story across the board: reliable three-point shooters for the Hawks couldn't get their shots to fall. Okongwu shot 2-of-7 from three, while Aaron Wiggins shot 1-of-6 from distance.

Turnovers were also a key feature in this game, with the Hawks committing 17 in total, off of which the Bulls scored 20 points. These turnovers, as Snyder often references along with getting stops, impact the Hawks' ability to establish their identity: it's key for Atlanta to get out on the run in transition/off of a miss and when the Hawks are committing turnovers this impacts the Hawks significantly.

"It's hard to stop the ball when you turn the ball over," said CJ McCollum postgame.

Chicago turnovers were also how the Hawks remained in this game, scoring 34 points off of the Bulls' 24 turnovers — without these, the Hawks would not have been able to close the margin as they did, with Johnson and McCollum credited for 10 points apiece off of Chicago turnovers.

In addition, when the Hawks are off form from three, they are at least able to rack up points in the paint — many of which came off of turnovers — scoring 66 points in the paint, with Johnson accounting for 20 of these. Johnson finished with 27 points on 11-of-26 shooting from the field to go with his triple-double.

The Hawks were chasing the game for much of the affair, but Snyder didn't believe that this pursuit tired the Hawks physically.

"I didn't feel like we were tired," said Snyder. "Powell hit some tough shots in the overtime which I thought we defended pretty well. We made a couple of adjustments that our guys executed that I thought were really good. You put yourself in a position where you've got to make a lot of plays. We made enough to go to get where we were, but the game goes back and forth, and it went back one too many times."

There's no doubt the Hawks left themselves with a lot of work to do, both in the first half and in the fourth quarter when they trailed by double-digits. But they had their chances in regulation, and it slipped through their fingers (well, quite literally in Wiggins' case). In overtime, the quality of Powell (33 points on 12-of-29 shooting) shone through as he seized the game, with enough support from the rest to see the Bulls through.

It's a poor loss for the Hawks, who would have won this game had they hit any number of their 26 missed threes in regulation. They were also off since Monday, while the Bulls were in action on Wednesday, so their flat start to the game looks worse with context. In the context of the NBA Cup, the Hawks still have a positive point differential and are still in play to advance but cannot afford another loss such as this.

The Hawks (7-6) are back in action on Sunday when they will encounter another team on the road desperate for victory: the 1-12 Milwaukee Bucks.

#2637. 5 things we learned after the Ohio State victory over Northwestern

It certainly wasn't a smooth walk through among the roses, but Ohio State got back in the win column after dropping two straight games when it beat Northwestern 28-19 on Saturday. The only time the Buckeyes trailed was when the Wildcats scored first on a field goal in the first quarter, but from there the Buckeyes had the lead despite several miscues and mental mistakes that surely frustrated all of Buckeye Nation.

In fact, the score made things look a little closer than it was after Ohio State fumbled while running the clock out, and then the Wildcats took the ball down and scored a touchdown on the last play of the game (sorry, bettors). At the end of the day, it was a win OSU needed badly just to get some positive momentum with a freshman running the show under center, and now it's time to build from here. Jeremiah Smith even added another record to his personal achievements.

After each Ohio State football game, we like to reflect on what we saw and what we can take away from the action, and so it is here too. Here are five things we think we learned about the Buckeyes after their 28-19 victory over Northwestern on Saturday.

Some of the mistakes we're seeing from this team are baffling, especially this late in the season. There are a lot of new guys becoming part of the culture and a lot of young guys trying to figure things out, but the list is pretty long on how many times the Buckeyes didn't keep their composure or simply made a bad play physically.

From Isaiah West fumbling the ball away while Ohio State was looking to run out the clock, to Legend Bey taunting the Northwestern sideline after he made several ridiculous moves for an eight-yard game, it made the game closer than it needed to be and could have spelled doom against a more talented opponent.

At this point, the team kind of is what it is, and I'm not sure these mistakes can all of a sudden turn off, but I guess we'll see.

Freshman backup quarterback Luke Fahey did show more composure this game as he continues to find his footing at one of the glamour positions of college football. It wasn't perfect by any means, but he seems to be gaining more confidence. Yes, he missed several throws and reads, but he finished the day 21-of-32 for 201 yards with three touchdowns and an interception.

Those stats aren't as good (arguably) as what he had in his first two starts, but he played better by looking for Jeremiah Smith more and by not taking so many check-downs. Ohio State still needs him to play even better, especially in Lincoln next week against Nebraska, but it was a step in the right direction.

That was more like it for the Ohio State defense. The late score made things look worse as the Buckeyes were playing softer coverage, but giving up 19 points after allowing 30 and 42 against USC and Oregon, respectively, is more of what we've come to expect from the OSU defense and Matt Patricia.

Northwestern was the second-leading rushing team in the Big Ten, and Ohio State allowed just 53 total yards on the ground in this one. And while the Wildcats have more success through the air than you'd expect, the fact that the offense and special teams put the OSU defense in a bad spot on more than one occasion, and the reality that Chip Kelly was on the other sideline, means we say good job in this one.

Yes, No. 4 is still the best player in college football, and we're glad to see that the Ohio State coaching staff decided to get in Fahey's ear and remind him of that. Smith had a lot more targets than last week and finished with 11 receptions for 117 yards (10.6 ypc) and a touchdown. Those aren't eye-popping, but they are very good numbers that should allow him to be on top of the Heisman race.

I always hated how voters cast their votes for the Heisman by putting too much emphasis on teams winning, the stats, and the position the player plays. In this case, there's little doubt that Smith is the best player in college football, so just make sure he gets to New York and wins the thing. There's a lot of attention being paid to him on a weekly basis, and he's still putting up better numbers than almost anyone else.

Putting the Scarlet and Gray uniform on is like being in a fishbowl. You are expected to win every game, sometimes by multiple scores, and when any of those two things don't happen, the local media and fans are all over this team. Heck, the Buckeyes hadn't lost three regular-season games and two in a row since 2011, so things are at a fever pitch in Columbus with head coach Ryan Day, the coaching staff, players, and maybe even the water boy coming under the gun.

By watching this game, it sure feels like the players are feeling it. There were several dropped passes or interceptions, some mental mistakes, and guys trying to do too much instead of relaxing and just doing their jobs and allowing the coaching and talent of others to take over. It feels like how Ohio State played against Michigan for about a three-year run, and there's no doubt the players are feeling the pinch of criticism. The men in the arena need to put that aside and just play free and loose.

#2635. Texans rule David Montgomery out for Sunday

Texans running back David Montgomery will not make his return to the lineup in Sunday’s game against the Browns.

Montgomery was listed as questionable to play on Friday’s injury report, but the Texans announced on Saturday that he will not travel with the team and has been ruled out. This will be the fourth straight game that he has missed with a groin injury.

The Texans also announced that cornerback Jaylin Smith (hamstring) will not be activated from injured reserve.

Linebacker Jake Hummel has been activated from injured reserve. He’s been out since Week 1 with a groin injury.

#2634. NFL Week 10 Injury Report: Kenneth Walker ruled out, Rhamondre Stevenson listed questionable

Staying up to date on NFL injury news is of the utmost importance for fantasy football success. The article below tracks all fantasy-relevant players currently listed on their team's injury report and provides fantasy managers with actionable recommendations as new information rolls in.

Check back for updates from Tuesday through Saturday.

**UPDATED AS OF SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 14 AT 4:30 PM ET**

Kincaid was limited but was removed from the injury report Friday. He will play against the Jets.

Impact: Likely none. Kincaid has played through injuries this season largely without issue.

Palmer managed only seven offensive snaps in Week 8 before departing with an aggravation of the hamstring injury he has battled since Week 4. He was placed on injured reserve.

Impact: Not much, honestly. Palmer has played sparingly this season in a situational role, although his absence could leave room for Skylar Bell to be active for the third time this season.

Achane suffered a torn ACL in the team's Week 3 loss to the Chiefs, ending his season.

Impact: Achane's unfortunate season-ending injury creates opportunity for Ollie Gordon and Jaylen Wright. The timing of the injury makes it likely that Achane is able to fully recover before the start of the 2027 regular season.

The Dolphins placed Willis on injured reserve in Week 10. He will be eligible to return in Week 14, but Willis is seeking a second opinion after the injury progressed into his abdomen. Season-ending surgery is possible.

Impact: Kyle McCord's installation as the team's starter hurts all involved. Until we see how McCord fares in this system, only Ollie Gordon is a safe FLEX starter.

Bell is listed as doubtful for Week 10 against the Colts.Impact: Bell has largely been unable to get anything going during his rookie season, with the team leaning more heavily on Malik Washington and Caleb Douglas. The rookie's expected absence could afford Kevin Coleman Jr. additional opportunities, although the low-volume Miami pass offense remains unlikely to support more than one pass catcher, now playing with a backup quarterback in Kyle McCord.

Doubs was placed on injured reserve following a shoulder injury sustained in Week 6. He will miss the next four games, at minimum.

Impact: The Patriots have now played only 33 offensive snaps with both Doubs and A.J. Brown on the field together this season after Doubs was injured on his second offensive snap in Week 6. Brown returned from injured reserve in Week 6 and should have the runway to return WR1 numbers while Doubs remains sidelined.

Brown has missed the previous two weeks with a "flare up" in his knee. The team announced Tuesday that he will travel to Germany for Week 10. He was limited to begin the week before drawing the questionable tag for Week 10.

Impact: DeMario Douglas, Kyle Williams, Mack Hollins, and Kyle Williams led the team in snaps and routes in the absence of Brown in Week 9, with none of the bunch consistent fantasy producers. Fantasy managers are likely forced to wait until late in the week to get a better sense of whether Brown will return in Week 10.

Henderson has been sidelined since Week 8 and will not play in Week 10 against the Lions.

Stevenson is reportedly set to miss "a short period of time" with a tendon issue in his knee, per ESPN's Adam Schefter. Even so, the veteran back drew the questionable tag for Week 10 against the Lions.

Impact: An absence from Stevenson could place the team in a dire situation with TreVeyon Henderson also sidelined for an indefinite time, likely leaving Corey Kiiner atop the depth chart for a matchup against the Lions in Germany. Kiner would gain viable FLEX status, should Stevenson miss. Lan Larison is his backup.

Henry played through this injury in Week 9, and was limited to begin Week 10. He was removed from the injury report Friday and will play against the Lions in Germany.

Wilson was ruled out for Week 9 Friday after failing to practice all week with a concussion. He was limited to begin Week 10, and head coach Aaron Glenn said he is "very hopeful" that Wilson will play. He officially drew the questionable tag for Week 10.

Impact: Adonai Mitchell could operate as the Jets' No. 1 wide receiver in his albeit volatile downfield role.

In Week 9, Cooper injured the same ankle that he hurt earlier this year, but he practiced in a limited capacity to begin Week 10. Despite drawing the questionable tag, he is expected to play.

Impact: Cooper is on track to play and warrants FLEX treatment against the Bills.

Mitchell is listed as questionable for Week 10 but is expected to play.Impact: Minimal. The downfield threat brings a wide range of outcomes on a weekly basis and makes for one of the more "yolo" starts in fantasy circles.

Jackson returned from an ankle injury in Week 8 and made it all of one offensive snap before suffering a thumb injury that is likely to sideline him for the remainder of the regular season.

Impact: Jackson's absence is the biggest hit to the fantasy value of alpha receiver Zay Flowers, who falls to a mid-range WR2 in rest of season rankings. Recent signee Jacoby Brissett is expected to start under center in Week 10.

Huntley suffered a season-ending turf toe injury in the team's Week 8 loss to the Bills.

Smythe suffered a torn Achilles in the team's Week 4 win over the Titans. His season is done.

Impact: It was Matt Hibner who saw the largest increase in snaps following Smythe's departure in Week 4, making it unlikely we see veteran Mark Andrews in a more robust role.

The Bengals placed Iosivas on injured reserve in Week 3. The team activated his 21-day practice window this week but he is listed as doubtful to play in Week 10 against the Steelers.

Impact: Wide receivers Colbie Young and Dohnte Meyers will duke it out for the No. 3 wide receiver role for at least the next four weeks. Meyers can be added in 14-team leagues, though his upside is questionable.

All suffered a torn ACL in Week 7. He was placed on injured reserve Tuesday and will miss the remainder of the regular season.

Impact: All loses yet another season in devastating fashion after suffering his third torn ACL. His absence could provide a slight uptick in snap rate and route participation for Mike Gesicki, although he will be a difficult weekly start for as long as both Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins remain healthy.

Fannin played through the injury in Week 9, but did not enter the box score until overtime. He was limited to begin Week 10 and removed from the injury report Friday.

Boston did not practice to begin Week 10, ultimately drawing the questionable tag.

Impact: Boston continues to deal with lower-leg injuries, but he played effectively last week. If he cannot face the Texans in Week 10, KC Concepcion and Fannin would benefit.

Impact: He will be eligible to return after four games missed.

Pittman was limited on Wednesday before being seen using a scooter in the locker room after practice. It was then revealed that Pittman aggravated his foot injury. Impact: Pittman's potential return could lower Germie Bernard's target share.

Marks was limited to begin Week 10 but was removed from the injury report Friday.

Dell was limited to begin Week 10 but removed from the injury report Friday.

Harrison was limited to begin Week 10. He was ruled out Friday.

Higgins saw his 2026 season taken from him due to a torn ACL suffered in camp.

Rodriguez played through the injury in Week 9 and remained limited early in Week 10. He was removed from the injury report Friday and will play against the Titans.

Meyers played through the injury in Week 9 and sat out the following Wednesday. He was removed from the injury report Friday and will play against the Titans.

Waddle suffered a concussion in the team's Week 9 win over the Panthers.

#2633. Josh Hart admits he’s ‘not in a good head space’as his Knicks struggles mount

INDIANAPOLIS — Josh Hart's issues aren't exclusive to his shot. The Knicks veteran said he's mentally struggling to start a disappointing season, and he doesn't know how to break out of it.

"Wish I could tell you," Hart said. "Don't know. Right now I'm not in a good head space and I got to figure out how to improve that. And improve my play."

Asked what that meant, Hart, who is shooting just 36 percent on the season, said, "Just mentally. Got to be better mentally. Got to figure stuff out."

Josh Hart of the New York Knicks shoots a 3-pointer against the Indiana Pacers in Indianapolis on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

Hart finished scoreless Friday night and was benched for the entire fourth quarter of a 106-104 loss to the Pacers, among the low points of a season that has never been on track for the 31-year-old.

He's up for an extension, but the Knicks put out a statement in October declaring they're shutting down all negotiations, including Hart's and Karl-Anthony Towns'.

Hart revealed Friday that he suffered a calf injury before training camp, which set back his conditioning. He then hurt his ankle and missed three games.

The Knicks are stacked with wings and guards, creating congestion and sporadic playing time. Mikal Bridges has also been benched, as coach Mike Brown leaned on Landry Shamet and Miles McBride.

Brown acknowledged that finding time for Bridges and Hart could be difficult.

Josh Hart, left, speaks with New York Knicks teammate Mikal Bridges during a game against the Indiana Pacers in Indianapolis on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

"There are several different ways you can look at it," Hart said. "You can look at it, if they have it going, cool. Good. You could look at it like, 'OK, maybe something else has to change.'"

Hart didn't specify the "change," but logic indicates he meant a trade. Three years ago, Leon Rose faced a similar conundrum. Too many guards, not enough minutes.

So Rose traded two — RJ Barrett and Immanuel Quickley — for a bigger forward in OG Anunoby.
